title: Building trust and resilience through secure software practices
snippet: Learn how Sage uses the Software Security Code of Practice to strengthen assurance, collaboration, and continuous improvement in the wider digital ecosystem. The post Building trust and resilience through secure software practices appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Sage used the UK Government’s Software Security Code of Practice to assess its established security, governance, and assurance practices across the Copilot Factory Framework (CFF).

The assessment showed that embedding security throughout software design, development, deployment, and maintenance helps create more resilient AI-powered services.

The assessment validated established security practices, including access reviews, third-party dependency controls, vulnerability management, and security documentation, while helping Sage make the supporting governance and evidence more explicit.

Cross-functional collaboration between Security, Product, Engineering, Architecture, and Cloud Operations provided a more complete view of how security controls are understood and applied across the software lifecycle.

Organisations can use the Software Security Code of Practice as a practical framework for continuous improvement, stronger customer assurance, and greater cyber resilience.

Digital services are central to how businesses manage finances, people, and operations. As reliance on software grows, and AI capabilities become embedded across more products, users need confidence that security is built into how the technology is designed, developed, and maintained.

At Sage, maintaining software security is part of our wider commitment to building trust and resilience.

As signatories of the UK Government’s Cyber Resilience Pledge and ambassadors of the Software Security Code of Practice, we’re committed to finding practical ways to test our security approach, learn from the process, and help promote stronger security across the wider software ecosystem, while encouraging our partners to do the same.

Here’s what we talk about in this article:

Why Sage supports the Cyber Resilience Pledge 

Cyber resilience is not only a technical priority. It is essential to business continuity, customer confidence, and responsible innovation. By supporting the Pledge and the Code, Sage is reinforcing its commitment to secure software practices and collaboration between government and industry. This collaboration helps translate shared security principles into practical action: government provides a clear and consistent framework, while industry applies it in real operating environments and shares practical insights to support its continued relevance and wider adoption.

Our involvement with the Code reflects our broader responsibility to contribute beyond our own organisation. By sharing practical experience, Sage can help other organisations understand how the Code can be applied, encourage partners to adopt stronger practices and provide constructive industry insight into how voluntary frameworks work in practice. This helps build a more consistent approach to software security across the wider ecosystem and keep the focus on sustained resilience rather than one-off compliance. 

The approach

Sage selected the Copilot Factory Framework (CFF) for assessment against the Software Security Code of Practice as it provides AI capabilities that can be used across multiple products. This made it a meaningful test of whether established security practices could be demonstrated consistently in a shared, fast-evolving technology environment.

The CFF provides a scalable foundation for delivering AI-powered experiences across Sage products, enabling teams to build and deploy AI capabilities using consistent governance, security controls, and approved technologies. Assessing a shared platform therefore offered value beyond a single service: it tested the foundations that product teams rely on when bringing AI capabilities to customers.

The assessment was not simply about confirming alignment with individual controls. It examined how security decisions, evidence, and responsibilities connect across the full lifecycle and whether that approach could provide clear assurance to the teams that depend on the CFF.

The assessment brought together colleagues from Security, Product, Engineering, Architecture and Cloud Operations.

A dedicated security lead coordinated the collection and validation of evidence, and an independent third party, NCC Group, reviewed the evidence against the Code’s controls.

The independent review confirmed established strengths and created a clear route for further improvement. In particular, it showed where greater clarity, formality, and consistency would make existing governance easier to apply, evidence, and understand across teams.

Key outcomes and lessons learned

Embedding security throughout design and development 

The review reinforced the importance of building security into design and development decisions for the CFF. This includes the consistent governance of third-party services, software components, dependencies, and licences from the outset, supported by clear and accessible evidence. Embedding these practices early strengthens traceability, supports compliance, and helps product teams identify and address software security risks before delivery.

Validating assurance around the build environment 

The review validated the controls that protect the integrity and security of the software build environment, including managed access, strong authentication, infrastructure-as-code, and audit logging. It also identified an opportunity to introduce greater formality and consistency through repeatable access reviews, providing ongoing assurance that access remains appropriate and aligned with business need.

Validating secure deployment and maintenance

The review considered how vulnerabilities are identified, prioritised, and managed throughout the software lifecycle. It validated the effectiveness of existing vulnerability management practices against the Software Security Code of Practice, including automated security scanning, penetration testing, and defined remediation targets. The outcome was stronger assurance that risks are addressed according to their significance and managed consistently throughout the lifecycle. For teams using the CFF, this provides greater confidence that vulnerabilities affecting a shared platform can be identified and acted on in a structured and timely way.

Clarifying service commitments

Because the CFF primarily provides AI services to other Sage products, some of the Code’s requirements needed to be considered in the context of internal product customers.

The review validated the service governance supporting the CFF, including established support and communication processes, lifecycle management, and commitments around service retirement. It also identified opportunities to express these practices with greater clarity and formality. This provides dependent teams with greater transparency and predictability, reduces operational risk, enables more effective planning, and supports reliable service delivery across the organisation.

Advice and insights for other organisations

For organisations considering using the Code, our experience highlighted four practical ways to gain greater value from the assessment:

Use the Code as a catalyst for improvement. The greatest value can come from the conversations the assessment creates and the opportunities it reveals. Clearly expressed governance and ownership can deliver greater clarity, accountability, and assurance. 

Formalise what already works. Strong practices may already exist, but clear ownership, documented commitments and accessible evidence make it easier to demonstrate that controls are operating as intended. 

Bring the right people together early. Software security spans more than one function. Involving Security, Product, Engineering, Architecture, and Cloud Operations creates a more complete view of how security is applied across the lifecycle. 

Share practical learning. Implementation experience can help other organisations apply the Code, support wider adoption, and strengthen resilience across the software ecosystem.

Final thoughts: Future commitments

The Software Security Code of Practice offers organisations a valuable opportunity to strengthen security, build customer trust, and demonstrate responsible leadership.

For organisations considering the Code, the first step is to assess how its principles align with existing practices, identify where ownership or evidence could be strengthened, and involve the right teams early. The wider opportunity is to use the assessment not only to improve internal assurance, but also to contribute practical insight that helps raise standards across the industry.

Sage continues to advocate for the Code beyond our own assessment by sharing practical expertise and encouraging participation across our partner ecosystem. This extends the value of government-industry collaboration: lessons learned from implementation can support wider adoption, strengthen collective resilience and demonstrate how common principles can be applied in different operating environments. Zynk’s adoption of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology’s Software Security Code of Practice shows how shared learning and advocacy can help extend common security principles through the wider partner ecosystem.

title: Everyday agentic AI: How Sage is reshaping the future of accounting with MTD
snippet: Agentic AI can plan, act, and flag issues for review. Find out how it helps accountants manage MTD for Income Tax, and how to prepare your practice. The post Everyday agentic AI: How Sage is reshaping the future of accounting with MTD appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Agentic AI is software that doesn’t just analyse data. It can plan actions, make decisions, and carry them out within limits that people set. For Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax, that means AI agents can help with repeatable, rules-based work—such as preparing data, flagging issues for review, and prompting client follow-ups—while accountants review and approve what is sent to HMRC, so they and bookkeepers have more time for judgement and advice.

Key takeaways

Agentic AI plans, acts, and makes decisions under human guidance, rather than only analysing data.

MTD for Income Tax adds workload: quarterly submissions, continuous data capture, and tighter reporting timelines. HMRC estimates around 1,077,000 more sole traders and landlords must join from April 2027, with the threshold falling again to £20,000 in April 2028.

The Sage MTD for Income Tax Agent, available now in Sage for Accountants, flags which clients are in scope, sets up quarterly jobs in advance and runs data checks before submission. Updates are submitted only once the accountant approves them.

There are no penalty points for late quarterly updates in 2026/27, but from 2027/28 a points-based regime applies: 4 points triggers a £200 penalty.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) generates the estimated tax calculations under MTD, so the accountant’s role shifts to validating and interpreting the figures.

Here’s what this article discusses:

Why does agentic AI matter for MTD for Income Tax?

Agentic AI matters for MTD for Income Tax because quarterly updates and continuous record-keeping add work that most practices don’t have the capacity for, and AI agents can take on the routine parts of it.

Agentic AI is transforming accounting and bookkeeping right now.

Across Sage, intelligent agents are already planning, reasoning, and acting alongside professionals—amplifying their expertise and unlocking new capacity.

The launch of the MTD for Income Tax Agent marks a decisive step change: routine preparation supported in the background, with accountants reviewing and approving the results, and more time for strategy, clients, and growth.

MTD is exposing a truth the profession already knows: accountants are running out of capacity.

Quarterly updates, digital record-keeping, and client demands are stretching firms further than ever before.

Practices are already under immense pressure. Rising client expectations, increased regulatory complexity, and squeezed margins leave little room for error. Finding enough time to maintain service levels is a daily challenge.

MTD for Income Tax brings a step change in workload: quarterly submissions, continuous data capture, and tighter reporting timelines. Practices must rethink how they manage client data, ensure accuracy, and deliver advice, at scale and speed.

And 2026 is only the start.

From April 2027, employers must report some benefits in kind—company cars, car fuel, vans, van fuel, and employer-provided medical benefits—through payroll in real time, with most other benefits following from April 2028 (GOV.UK). Companies House has also confirmed that, from April 2028, all companies must file their annual accounts using commercial software (GOV.UK).

Practices will face an unprecedented surge in client queries and additional admin, all while talent remains tight and margins thin.

That surge has already started. Since September 2026, HMRC has been signing up sole traders and landlords it believes should already be using MTD for Income Tax but haven’t registered. HMRC writes to these taxpayers directly and doesn’t copy in their agents, so practices are fielding questions about letters they haven’t seen. HMRC’s records are based on historic tax returns, so some letters will relate to businesses that have stopped trading or clients who may be exempt (ATT).

Without automation and AI support, many small and mid-sized firms risk reaching breaking point.

This is where agentic AI makes the difference.

It can support the repeatable, rules-based work—preparing reconciliations, flagging issues, and prompting follow-ups—freeing up human capacity for judgement and strategy, while accountants stay responsible for checking and approving what is submitted.

As Chris Downing, Director for accountants and bookkeepers at Sage, said at Accountex North in 2025, before MTD for Income Tax began:

“In a few months, MTD for Income Tax will become a reality. More deadlines, more conversations, but also an opportunity—an opportunity to simplify, create capacity, anticipate and automate the work we do.”

Chris Downing, Director for accountants and bookkeepers at Sage

AI agents for MTD matter because they lay the groundwork for an AI-first future, helping firms build confidence in automation, spot anomalies faster, and create capacity when they’ll need it most.

What changes are coming for accounting practices?

Emma Rawson, Director of Public Policy at the Association of Taxation Technicians, also speaking at a keynote at Accountex North, said that 12 months earlier, the profession was still being convinced MTD was happening.

“Now the conversation has shifted to readiness: software choices, client planning, and thorny real-world questions.”

Emma Rawson, Director of Public Policy at the Association of Taxation Technicians

Accounting and bookkeeping face key collision points on the horizon:

Change

What it means for practices

When

MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates

The first quarterly updates were due by 7 August 2026 for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000

From April 2026

MTD for Income Tax threshold expansion

New bands bring many more clients into scope. HMRC estimates around 1,077,000 more sole traders and landlords must join from April 2027 at the £30,000 threshold. Clients can also sign up voluntarily

April 2027 (£30,000); April 2028 (£20,000)

MTD for Income Tax penalties

No penalty points for missed quarterly update deadlines in 2026/27, but all four updates must still be sent before the tax return can be submitted. From 2027/28, each missed quarterly deadline earns a point. At 4 points a £200 penalty applies, plus £200 for each further missed deadline

2026/27 easement; points from the 2027/28 tax year

Payrolling of benefits in kind

Mandatory real-time reporting through payroll, starting with company cars, fuel, vans, and medical benefits

April 2027; most other benefits from April 2028

Companies House digital filing

All companies must file annual accounts using commercial software, ending web and paper filing for accounts

From April 2028

VAT cycles

Overlapping workloads, most often quarterly, that test practice capacity

Year-round

Quarterly updates are a digital handshake to HMRC. They don’t crystallise a tax liability, but they build a habit of working digitally and keep clients closer to real-time information.

Chris Downing, Director for accountants and bookkeepers, Sage

Downing calls out the “hidden work” that clients never see—the chasing, corrections, and compliance housekeeping that consume hours every week.

These aren’t side issues. They’re the silent drain on growth and service quality.

The takeaway:

Accountants aren’t short on deadlines. They’re short on capacity.

Capacity creation isn’t a side effect of automation. It’s the strategy.

Agentic workflows are how you get there

What is the Sage MTD for Income Tax Agent?

The Sage MTD for Income Tax Agent supports set-up and quarterly update preparation for MTD for Income Tax, while accountants review and approve what is submitted.

The MTD for Income Tax Agent was announced at Accountex North.

Accountants decide where the review points sit, and anything ambiguous is routed to a person for review. The exact configuration options depend on the current release.

Here, AI thinks in workflows rather than single tasks:

Preparation and authorisation: The agent anticipates what needs doing and prompts action, such as reminding you to move client authorisations into the HMRC Agent Services Account (ASA), linking organisations to individuals, and verifying authority. Authorisation with HMRC is then completed manually through the official ASA.

Guardrails by design: You decide where review points sit, and anything ambiguous is routed for human review. Nothing is submitted to HMRC until the accountant approves it.

Quarterly updates with context: Instead of repetitive data entry, the MTD for Income Tax Agent reviews incoming information, highlights anomalies, requests missing items, and can submit updates once the accountant gives the green light.

A guided client experience: For do-it-for-me clients who won’t adopt software, the agent provides simple, repeatable approval and upload flows, while your default motion remains bringing clients into software for full visibility.

As Georgina Timothy, Director of Product Management, Sage for Accountants, explained: “We’ll automate the end-to-end workflow, but you stay in control. The agent takes care of the heavy lifting so you can focus on your clients.”

This isn’t testing the waters. It’s a real leap into agentic workflows purpose-built for MTD, a signal of what the next decade will look like.

Intelligent systems can support background processes such as authorisation prompts, data checks, and preparing submissions for approval, while accountants move up a layer into proactive, insight-driven work.

The shift goes deeper. As HMRC redefines how tax is calculated and reported, automation will change not just how work gets done, but what “doing the work” really means.

The May 2026 release of the MTD for Income Tax Agent takes on more of the quarterly set-up work. It:

flags which sole trader clients are in scope for quarterly reporting

matches HMRC income sources to client records using National Insurance numbers

sets up quarterly reporting jobs in advance, so work starts before each deadline

shows data checks before anything is submitted

keeps the whole MTD workflow in one hub

The agent isn’t fully autonomous. Accountants stay in control of review and submission.

As Lisa Ewens, SVP Product, Small Business & Accountants at Sage, explained: “The MTD for Income Tax Agent anticipates the work practices need to complete each quarter and prepares it in advance. It draws on Sage’s deep accounting expertise and trusted financial data to keep accountants firmly in control, handling the administration so they can focus on the judgement work that only they can do.”

For Gary Beeby of Beeby-England, a practice using the agent, the change is in where the work starts: “Instead of starting from scratch, we can focus on reviewing the work and refining it for our clients.”

How does MTD for Income Tax change client tax returns?

Under MTD for Income Tax, HMRC generates estimated tax calculations from the quarterly data submitted through software, and your role shifts from generating the numbers to validating and interpreting them.

MTD digitalises and redefines the tax return.

In the new model, HMRC generates estimated tax calculations based on quarterly data submitted through the software.

However, the annual tax return still needs human checks. Where you act as the client’s main agent, you check the calculation, share the proposed return with your client, get their written confirmation that it’s correct and complete, and then submit it through compatible software. Your client remains responsible for their tax affairs.

You will need to accept your role shifting from generating the numbers to validating and interpreting them.

“The software providers aren’t doing the tax calculation,” explained Downing. “HMRC is. Your job becomes validating and reconciling that information, making sure what HMRC holds matches what your clients have.”

A fundamental change in accountability

Compatible software can help surface missing information, support reconciliation of Pay As You Earn (PAYE), Construction Industry Scheme (CIS), and other data sources, and support end-year adjustments through the business source adjustable summary (BSAS)—the mechanism that ties quarterly updates to final tax adjustments so client records and HMRC’s view stay in sync.

That means less time keying in figures and more time shaping what those figures mean.

The tax return era is evolving into a continuous data exchange—a living process rather than a one-time event.

And that shift sets the stage for the next evolution: agentic workflows that not only automate but anticipate how and when that work gets done.

How can your practice prepare for agentic AI? Five steps

Whether you’re already experimenting with AI assistants or working through MTD for Income Tax, the five steps are the same: segment and sequence your clients, digitise records early, automate the quarterly cycle, price your new service model, and reinvest the capacity you create.

1. Segment and sequence

Start with your £50,000+ sole traders and landlords, who are already using MTD for Income Tax, then plan for clients above £30,000 who join in April 2027:

Check who HMRC has already signed up. Since September 2026, HMRC has been enrolling taxpayers it believes should be using MTD for Income Tax for 2026/27. Review client records in your Agent Services Account, and flag anyone who has stopped trading or may be exempt. Clients joining from April 2027 or April 2028 still need to sign up themselves or through you.

Segment clients by their preferred working style.

This segmentation isn’t only operational. It’s strategic. It determines how far you automate, how you price, and where you’ll free the most capacity.

For a quarter-by-quarter plan, read Help! MTD for Income Tax has started! A practice plan for the year ahead.

For what to do when HMRC signs up a client, read HMRC-led sign-up for MTD for Income Tax: What accountants need to know.

2. Digitise records early

Don’t wait for MTD to force the issue:

Move laggards onto digital bookkeeping as soon as possible: cloud ledgers for sole traders, bridging or prep tools for CSV and bank-only clients.

Every early migration compounds the benefit: smoother quarterly updates, fewer manual reconciliations, and a cleaner testing ground for AI-driven workflows.

3. Automate the quarterly cycle

Start shaping how automation will fit into your workflow.

Identify which tasks your team can safely hand over to automation when available: data reviews, report generation, and client chases.

Work back from HMRC’s four fixed deadlines (7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May) to flatten peaks and establish a repeatable rhythm.

Remember, automation isn’t about speed; it’s about flow—turning four mini tax seasons into one.

Use 2026/27 to get the rhythm right. There are no penalty points for late quarterly updates this tax year, but from 2027/28 missed deadlines count towards the 4-point penalty threshold.

The next quarterly deadline is 7 November 2026. For the 2026/27 tax year, the cycle runs as follows:

Quarterly period (standard quarters)

Quarterly update due

6 April – 5 July 2026

7 August 2026

6 July – 5 October 2026

7 November 2026

6 October 2026 – 5 January 2027

7 February 2027

6 January – 5 April 2027

7 May 2027

2026/27 tax return

31 January 2028

Each update is cumulative, covering the tax year to date. Clients who choose calendar quarters (ending 30 June, 30 September, 31 December and 31 March) have the same update deadlines (GOV.UK).

For a step-by-step process, read MTD quarterly updates: A practice guide for accountants and bookkeepers.

Block out your quarter-end weeks now. This isn’t four mad months and eight quiet ones—it’s a continuous rhythm.

Rebecca Benneyworth, Rebecca Benneyworth & Co

4. Price your new service model

MTD isn’t simply a compliance shift. It’s a pricing one:

Package quarterly reviews and year-end reconciliations into modern, data-driven service tiers.

Publish clear scope, service levels, and value communication so clients see the benefit of your automation investment.

Update letters of engagement and schedules of work now, while the transition window allows flexibility.

For example pricing tiers, read Pricing for MTD: How to charge more, and prove it’s worth it.

5. Reinvest the capacity you create

This is where automation pays off:

Ring-fence the hours you free for cash flow check-ins, tax-planning nudges, and advisory conversations.

Use quarterly cycles as the backbone for more frequent, proactive engagement, of the kind that builds client trust and long-term revenue.

Protect that dividend: calendar the time you win back, or it will vanish.

Real clients love quarterly tax forecasts. They know it’s indicative, but it stops the ‘I haven’t got the money’ conversation – and turns forecasting into an advisory moment.

Rebecca Benneyworth

With MTD for Income Tax now under way, and more clients joining in April 2027 and April 2028, you can use it as a test to perfect agentic AI processes.

Start small, document what works, and keep that one principle in mind: capacity creation isn’t a by-product of automation; it’s the goal.

Final thoughts: Authentic Intelligence, in practice

This isn’t AI for AI’s sake.

It’s Authentic Intelligence—people and agents, each doing what they’re best at.

Agents give you back time. You decide how to use it, whether that’s for judgement, relationships, or growth.

The question isn’t how we cope with more deadlines. It’s what we do with our capacity. Spend more time with clients. Spend more time thinking about strategy. Use that time to grow your practice.

Chris Downing

That’s the real promise of agentic AI: not replacing accountants and bookkeepers, but expanding what you can achieve.

MTD is the test case. Authentic Intelligence is the destination.

title: Plastic Packaging Tax: What businesses need to know, including 2027 updates
snippet: Are you affected by the Plastic Packaging Tax? Discover who's affected, and how, plus what's required to register and file tax returns. Changes are coming in 2027, and we detail those, too. The post Plastic Packaging Tax: What businesses need to know, including 2027 updates appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
The UK government is understandably keen for businesses and consumers to use recycled materials wherever possible.

Plastic Packaging Tax (PPT) has applied since April 2022 to certain plastic packaging components manufactured in or imported into the UK.

It’s being updated in 2027 in some key ways that businesses subject to the tax need to know.

Here’s how to check if your business need to register, what to report, and what changes you need to know about.

Here’s what we cover:

Planned since 2018, the Plastic Packaging Tax is a flagship UK government scheme and a key part of its environmental and sustainability planning.

It came into effect on 1 April 2022.

As its name suggests, it imposes a tax on UK businesses for the manufacture or import of plastic packaging with less than 30% recycled content.

In a brief summary, the rules and what you need to know are as follows:

Businesses should assess each finished component separately. If plastic accounts for more of the component’s weight than any other single substance, the component is treated as plastic packaging.

Components containing at least 30% recycled plastic are not chargeable, but they still count towards the registration threshold and require supporting evidence.

For components manufactured in or imported into the UK from 1 April 2026, PPT is charged at £228.82 per tonne where the component contains less than 30% recycled plastic.

Businesses are encouraged to make it clear if the Plastic Packaging Tax applies.

There is no mandatory requirement to state on an invoice that PPT has been paid. HMRC encourages liable businesses to share relevant information with business customers. But the government would like businesses to engage with customers about the use of recycled materials.

PPT returns are filed quarterly.

PPT is paid by the liable manufacturer or importer and is not charged separately to customers in the way VAT is. A business may choose to reflect the cost in its selling price.

Where PPT is reflected in the selling price, that cost forms part of the consideration on which VAT is calculated under the normal VAT rules.

Different rules apply where components are exported in the accounting period, are intended for export within 12 months, or are exported or converted into other plastic packaging components after PPT has been paid.

Deferral and credits are subject to statutory conditions, evidence and timing requirements. A credit claim must normally be made within two years of the tax becoming chargeable.

When did Plastic Packaging Tax start, and when are returns due?

PPT took effect on 1 April 2022.

Only finished plastic packaging components manufactured in or imported into the UK on or after that date fall within the PPT regime.

The tax returns are quarterly, which is to say they cover four accounting periods each year. These are:

1 April to 30 June

1 July to 30 September

1 October to 31 December

1 January to 31 March

It isn’t possible for a business to choose its own accounting periods.

Businesses should submit each return, and pay any tax due, by the last working day of the month following the end of the accounting period.

Is my business affected by the Plastic Packaging Tax?

Businesses must register if they expect to manufacture or import 10 tonnes or more of finished plastic packaging components in the next 30 days, or have manufactured or imported 10 tonnes or more in the previous 12 months.

The threshold is a registration trigger, not a tax-free allowance. Components containing at least 30% recycled plastic and other non-chargeable components may still count towards it.

Businesses must notify HMRC within 30 days of becoming liable to register. The liability date, and the date from which tax applies to chargeable components, depends on whether the forward-looking or backward-looking test is met.

How do I register for the Plastic Packaging Tax?

Businesses should use HMRC’s registration service with their business details, relevant packaging-weight estimate, applicable reference number, and Government Gateway credentials.

An agent acting on a business’s behalf can be authorised after the business registers, but cannot complete its initial registration.

Once registered, your business will be assigned a reference number that you should use in correspondence.

Records that businesses need to keep for the Plastic Packaging Tax

Once registered, businesses should keep supporting records by product line for at least six years from the end of the relevant accounting period.

In summary, the records are:

Weight details of each plastic packaging component.

Details of the weight of plastic packaging exported, if applicable.

Evidence of recycled content, including how you’ve worked out the percentage of recycled plastic for your business, its source, and what product lines the content is used with.

Evidence of why an exemption applies (e.g. packaging for medicine used for human medical products).

Accounts may record metric weights in tonnes, kilograms and grams. Return weights must be stated in kilograms and rounded down to the nearest whole kilogram.

Notably, your business should keep records even if it’s below the threshold.

This is because the threshold is a rolling 12-month time period, so your business could hit the limit and be liable to keep records and pay tax.

What needs to be included on Plastic Packaging Tax returns?

Businesses must report the relevant weights of finished plastic packaging components manufactured in or imported into the UK, including applicable recycled-content and exemption categories, exports and components intended for export.

The business must also include relevant credits and the tax due. Check HMRC’s current return guidance for the fields required for each accounting period.

What changes for the Plastic Packaging Tax rules in 2027?

A significant change to the PPT rules will take effect from 1 April 2027. Drinks businesses should also prepare separately for the deposit return schemes due to start in October 2027

Pre-consumer plastic

From 1 April 2027, pre-consumer plastic will no longer qualify as recycled plastic for PPT purposes.

A mass-balance approach will be available for qualifying chemically recycled plastic, subject to the applicable certification, attribution, record-keeping and evidence requirements.

Businesses should review supplier evidence and HMRC’s final operational guidance before the changes take effect.

Deposit return scheme

From 1 October 2027, eligible single-use polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic, aluminium and steel drinks containers holding between 150ml and 3 litres will fall within the deposit return scheme in England and Northern Ireland, with aligned but separately legislated arrangements in Scotland.

The scheme operator has announced a refundable 20p deposit for each eligible container in England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.

If your business manufactures or imports drinks packaging, assess your PPT position and deposit scheme role separately.

Check the final rules for every UK nation in which drinks are supplied, particularly Wales.

Tips to help you manage the Plastic Packaging Tax

Managing PPT requires practical planning and a clear view of a business’s packaging, suppliers, evidence and reporting processes.

These steps can help businesses maintain compliance and prepare for the 2027 changes:

Understand the detail of the legislation. Like most taxes, the Plastic Packaging Tax sounds simple on the surface but contains myriad details that can catch out the unwary. HMRC has plenty of information to help businesses gain clarity on what’s required.

Do a dry run. If the tax applies to your business, and you can spare the resources, try applying the detail of the tax to a previous quarter. This will help you create processes and, of course, work out your likely liability.

Final thoughts on Plastic Packaging Tax

If your business is new to the PPT, check both registration tests, map packaging by component, keep evidence of recycled content and build a quarterly reporting routine.

Drinks businesses should also assess their deposit return scheme duties before October 2027.

title: Cash flow forecast template for UK businesses: Free download now
snippet: A cash flow forecast shows what money you expect to come in and go out of your business, so you can spot potential shortfalls earlier. Find out how to build and update one, and download our free UK cash flow forecast template to get started. The post Cash flow forecast template for UK businesses: Free download now appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Running a business means knowing what money is coming in and what’s going out, not just today but also in the weeks and months ahead.

A cash flow forecast gives you that visibility. For sole traders, freelancers, and growing SMEs, that’s often the difference between staying afloat and running into trouble.

Key takeaways

A cash flow forecast estimates the money you expect to come in and go out over a set period, so you can spot shortfalls before they happen.

Unlike a profit forecast, it tracks when cash actually moves through your bank account, which is why a profitable business can still run short.

Record income when it’s likely to arrive, not when you invoice, and only include confirmed work.

The free template has dedicated rows for VAT, PAYE and corporation tax. Use only the rows that apply to your business.

Most small businesses update their forecast monthly, or weekly if cash is tight or income is irregular.

Cash flow pressure remains a real issue for businesses. According to Coface’s 2025 UK Payment Survey, 90% of UK companies surveyed experienced late payments in the past year, and 44% said payment delays were becoming more frequent. Government-commissioned research published in July 2025 estimates that late payments contribute to around 14,000 UK business closures each year, the equivalent of around 38 every day.

A cash flow forecasting template won’t prevent every problem, but it gives you the information you need to spot a potential issue before it becomes a crisis.

This guide explains what a cash flow forecast is, why it matters, and how to use one. You can also download the free cash flow forecast template below and start filling it in straight away.

Here’s what we’ll cover in the article:

What is a cash flow forecast?

A cash flow forecast is a forward-looking document that estimates how much money you expect to come in and go out of your business over a set period. It predicts whether you’ll have enough cash to cover your costs at any given point, before you get there.

A forecast isn’t a record of what happened – it’s a projection of what’s likely to happen, based on what you know today about your income and outgoings. That’s what makes it useful.

Most small businesses will run a forecast covering anywhere from one month to 12 months ahead, and update it regularly as their circumstances change.

These two are often confused, and the difference matters.

A profit forecast looks at whether your business is making more money than it’s spending overall. It’s based on revenue earned and costs incurred, regardless of when the cash actually moves.

A cash flow forecast, or cash flow projection, looks at when money physically enters and leaves your bank account. A business can be profitable on paper and still run into serious trouble if customers pay late, a large tax bill lands at the wrong time, or costs fall in a month when income is thin.

A straightforward example: you complete a project in March and invoice for £5,000. Your profit forecast includes £5,000 in March. But if your client pays in May, your cash flow forecast won’t show that money until it actually arrives. In the meantime, you still have rent, wages, and supplier payments to cover. This is why profitable businesses can and do run into cash flow problems. Understanding how your cash flow forecasting works in practice is just as important as the numbers themselves.

Why cash flow forecasting is important for small businesses

Most financial problems don’t arrive without warning. They build up gradually, and a forecast gives you the chance to spot them early enough to do something about it.

Avoiding cash shortfalls

A shortfall happens when your outgoings exceed your available cash, even temporarily. For a small business, that can mean missing payroll, defaulting on a supplier payment, or being unable to take on new work because you can’t cover the upfront costs. Forecasting doesn’t prevent shortfalls, but it tells you they’re coming. That gives you time to act, whether that means chasing an outstanding invoice, negotiating later payment of a supplier’s bill, or exploring suitable funding options, where appropriate, and seeking professional advice if you’re unsure.

Planning for tax payments

Whether you need to pay VAT, PAYE, or corporation tax, and how much and when, depends on your business’s specific circumstances. Not every business will have all three obligations, and filing and payment timetables can differ. Where they apply, a decent forecast can help you estimate roughly when they’re due and how much they’ll be. The problem for many small businesses is that these payments aren’t built into day-to-day cash planning, so they land as a surprise.

The free cash flow forecast template includes dedicated rows for VAT to HMRC, PAYE to HMRC, and corporation tax, so these obligations sit alongside your other outgoings rather than being an afterthought. Use only the rows that apply to your business.

Managing growth

Growth costs money before it makes money. Taking on a new member of staff or investing in equipment requires cash upfront, often before the revenue from that investment comes through.

A forecast lets you test whether your cash position can support a decision before you commit to it. That isn’t a reason to avoid growth, but to time it better.

Making informed decisions

The quality of a business decision is only as good as the information behind it. If you’re weighing up a new supplier or preparing for a quieter month, a regularly updated forecast gives you a factual basis to work from.

How to use the cash flow forecast template

The cash flow projection template is straightforward to set up.

Enter your company name, choose your period type (weekly, fortnightly or monthly), set your start date, and enter the number of periods you want to forecast across. Then work through the income and expenditure rows, filling in what you expect for each period.

Here’s how to approach each section.

Estimate your cash coming in

Start with your income. The cash flow forecast template for Excel gives you customer or sales channel rows, which you can label however makes sense for your business. A freelancer might use them for different clients. A product business might split them by sales channel.

Also include:

Expected loan or funding receipts if you’re waiting on finance

Any tax refunds you’re anticipating

Other one-off receipts that will land in a specific period

If your payment terms are 30 days, build that delay into your forecast.

List your cash going out

Work through the expenditure rows and enter your expected outgoings for each period. The template covers the most common costs for UK businesses, including:

Staff and payroll

Supplier and contractor payments

PAYE, VAT, and corporation tax to HMRC

Rent, utilities, and office costs

Insurance, subscriptions, and professional fees

For tax rows, enter the amounts in the period they are actually due to leave your account, not the period they relate to.

Review your opening and closing balances

Once your income and expenditure amounts are in place, then the cash flow summary at the bottom does the work. Your opening balance for the first period is the only figure you enter manually.

From there, the template automatically calculates your net cash flow and closing balance for each period, carrying the closing balance forward as the opening balance for the next period.

A positive closing balance means you expect to have cash available. A negative closing balance is a warning sign that needs attention before that period arrives.

Update your forecast regularly

A forecast you fill in once and never revisit loses its value quickly. As actual figures come in, update your template to reflect what really happened and adjust your projections forward.

How often you update depends on your situation. A business with tight cash flow or irregular income may need to review weekly. For most small businesses, a monthly update is enough to stay on top of things.

Monitor forecasted cash flows against actual cash flows

Updating your forecast is only half the job. The other half is comparing what you projected against what actually happened.

Each time you close out a period, go back to your forecast and fill in the real figures alongside your estimates. If your actual income came in lower than expected, or a cost ran higher than planned, note it and adjust your projections going forward.

Over time, this habit makes your forecasts more accurate. You start to see patterns, and you can build those realities into your numbers rather than working from assumptions that don’t reflect how your business works.

Cash flow forecast example

To see how the forecast works in practice, here is a simple example using a sole trader who runs a small landscaping business.

Opening balance: £2,500

In May, the business has two confirmed jobs worth £1,800 and £1,200 respectively. Based on 14-day payment terms, both payments are expected to land within the month. Total expected income for May: £3,000.

Outgoings for the same period:

Supplier payments (plants, materials): £800

Fuel and travel: £150

Public liability insurance (monthly portion): £45

HMRC VAT payment due in May: £600

Other costs: £80

Total expected expenditure: £1,675

Net cash flow: £3,000 minus £1,675 = £1,325

Closing balance: £2,500 plus £1,325 = £3,825

On paper, May looks healthy. But now imagine the client with the £1,200 job pays 30 days late.

The income drops to £1,800 for the month, the expenditure stays the same, and the net cash inflow falls to £125. The closing balance drops to £2,625.

The forecast doesn’t change the situation, but it tells you about it before it happens. That’s the value of running the numbers in advance.

If you know in April that May could be tight, you could ask for a deposit upfront, chase receivables early, or make sure you have enough in reserve to cover it.

How often should you update a cash flow forecast?

There is no single right answer, and it depends on your business. The more variable your income and outgoings, the more frequently you need to review your numbers.

Weekly updates

Weekly works best if your cash position is tight, your income is irregular, or you’re in the early stages of trading. Reviewing every week gives you enough time to react if something looks off, whether that’s a payment that hasn’t arrived or an unexpected cost landing earlier than planned.

Monthly updates

For most small businesses, a monthly update is enough. You review what actually came in and went out during the month, update your projections for the periods ahead, and adjust for anything that has changed. It should become a routine part of closing out the month rather than a separate task.

Rolling forecasts

A rolling forecast means you always maintain a set window of visibility ahead, typically 12 months, moving forward as each period passes. Rather than forecasting to a fixed year-end and starting again, you add a new period each time one closes.

This approach suits businesses that are growing, planning investment, or operating in sectors where conditions change quickly. It takes more discipline to maintain, but it gives you a more accurate picture over time.

Common cash flow forecasting mistakes to avoid

Even if you forecast regularly, it’s easy to fall into habits that make your numbers less reliable. These are the ones you should watch out for.

Overestimating income

Overestimating income is one of the most common forecasting mistakes for small businesses, and often the most damaging. It’s easy to forecast based on what you hope will come in, rather than what you can realistically expect.

If you’re quoting for three projects but only one is confirmed, only the confirmed one belongs in your forecast.

The same applies to timing. If a client has 30-day payment terms, don’t record the income on the day you invoice. Record it when the money is likely to land in your account.

Forgetting VAT and tax bills

Where VAT, PAYE, and corporation tax apply to your business, they can still catch you off guard. They don’t feel like everyday expenses, and the cash to cover them has often been spent by the time the bill arrives.

The template includes dedicated rows for each of these tax costs. Use the rows that apply to your business. If you’re unsure how VAT works for your business, it’s worth getting clear on your obligations before they affect your cash position.

Not updating your forecast

A forecast built in January and left untouched through March is no longer a forecast. It’s a record of what you expected three months ago. As your circumstances change, your numbers should change with them.

Set a regular time each week or month to review and update. It doesn’t have to take long, but it has to happen consistently to be useful.

Ignoring seasonal changes

Most businesses have periods that are busier or quieter than others. If your forecast treats every month the same, it won’t reflect reality.

Build seasonal patterns into your projections from the start, even if your estimates are rough. You can refine them as you gather more data over time.

Using invoice dates instead of payment dates

This is a common oversight, particularly for small businesses new to forecasting. Your forecast should reflect when cash actually moves, not when you raise an invoice or receive a bill.

If you issue an invoice today on 30-day terms, that income belongs in next month’s forecast, not this one.

How accounting software takes the guesswork out of cash flow

A spreadsheet works well when your finances are straightforward. But as your business grows and transactions increase, keeping a manual forecast accurate becomes a job in itself. Here’s how software helps:

Your figures update as things happen: Where connected features are available and set up correctly, software can bring your invoices, expenses, and bank transactions into one place, so your cash position reflects more up-to-date information rather than what you entered last week.

Tax figures are easier to estimate: Rather than working out your VAT, PAYE, or corporation tax rows entirely by hand, accounting software may help you estimate, track, and organise tax-related figures from the data you enter, depending on the product, your setup, and your circumstances. You should still check these figures against HMRC guidance or with an accountant before relying on them.

Late payments are easier to spot: When an invoice goes overdue and your invoicing and bank data are kept up to date, you can more easily see how it affects your projected closing balance. For small businesses where one late payment can shift an entire month’s numbers, that early visibility can give you time to act.

Forecasting becomes part of running the business: When your data is live and connected, staying on top of your cash flow stops being a separate monthly task and becomes a natural part of how you manage day to day.

If you want to see how that works in practice, Sage Accounting brings your invoicing, expenses, banking, and tax obligations together in one place.

Frequently asked questions

			

			

	

What’s the difference between a cash flow forecast and a cash flow statement?

	

			

A cash flow forecast is forward-looking. You use it to project what you expect to come in and go out over a future period.

A cash flow statement is historical. It records what actually happened to cash in your business and forms part of your formal financial accounts.

One helps you plan ahead. The other tells you what occurred.

		

	

	

How far ahead should a cash flow forecast go?

	

			

One month gives you enough visibility to manage immediate cash needs. Three months works better for planning decisions like hiring, supplier negotiations, or upcoming tax bills.

If you’re seeking funding or managing growth, maintain a 12-month forecast and update it monthly so the window always stays a year ahead.

		

	

	

Can I use a cash flow forecast for a start-up?

	

			

Yes, and it may be the single most important financial document you produce at that stage. Map out when you expect customers to pay, what your fixed costs look like, and how long your funding will last.

Lenders and investors may ask for it, and it helps you agree on workable payment terms with clients and suppliers from the start.

Your early figures will be estimates, and that’s fine. The discipline of building and updating the forecast is what matters.

		

	

	

Do I need a cash flow forecast for a loan or funding application?

	

			

Many lenders and investors may ask for one. It shows you understand your numbers, that you’ve thought through how the funding will be used, and you have a realistic repayment plan. The free cash flow forecast template above can give you a starting point, but lenders or investors may require additional information, specific formats, or professionally prepared forecasts.

	

	

Can ChatGPT make a cash flow forecast?

	

			

LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can generate a structure or populate a template, but they have no access to your actual business data. Unless you upload your actual numbers, any figures it produces are fabricated or based on generic assumptions with no relation to your real income or costs.

Do not upload sensitive business or customer data to any AI tool unless you are satisfied it is appropriate to do so and you understand how the tool will use, store, and protect that data.

		

	

		

	

This article was verified by a UK-based Accountant in September 2026. Accounting rules are complex and change frequently and we recommend you seek any accounting advice from a qualified accountant or tax professional. This template and guidance are for general information only and do not constitute accounting, tax, legal or financial advice. Tax obligations, payment dates and available reliefs depend on your business structure, registration status, accounting period and circumstances. Check the latest HMRC guidance or speak to a qualified accountant or tax adviser before relying on figures for tax, funding or business decisions.

title: Making Tax Digital for VAT deadlines
snippet: Your MTD for VAT Return is due one calendar month and seven days after your VAT period ends. Here are the key dates and a checklist to help you file on time. The post Making Tax Digital for VAT deadlines appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Under Making Tax Digital (MTD) for VAT, your VAT Return is due one calendar month and seven days after the end of each VAT period, and you must file it using MTD-compatible software. The rules have applied to all VAT-registered businesses since April 2022.

Key takeaways

Your VAT Return is due one calendar month and seven days after the end of your VAT period (the Annual Accounting Scheme has its own deadlines).

MTD for VAT has applied to all VAT-registered businesses since April 2022, and HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) signs up new VAT registrations automatically.

Digital links have been mandatory since April 2021, so you can’t copy and paste between your VAT records.

Late returns earn penalty points. The late return that takes you to your points threshold triggers a £200 penalty, and each further late return while you’re at the threshold can trigger another £200 penalty.

MTD for Income Tax began in April 2026, while MTD for Corporation Tax was cancelled in July 2025.

In April 2022, MTD for VAT was extended to significantly more businesses.

Those who have voluntarily registered for VAT need to follow its rules, including businesses below the VAT registration threshold.

If you’re VAT-registered, you need to understand the deadlines and meet them.

Here’s what this article discusses:

What are the key MTD for VAT deadlines?

Your VAT Return and payment are usually due one calendar month and seven days after the end of your VAT period.

Item

Key date or requirement

VAT Return deadline

One calendar month and seven days after the end of your VAT period

Annual Accounting Scheme

Return normally two months after the end of an accounting period of 4 to 12 months, or one month after the end of a period shorter than four months

Payment deadline

Usually the same as the return deadline under standard VAT accounting. Annual Accounting Scheme instalments and balancing payments, and payments on account, have separate dates. If you pay by Direct Debit, HMRC collects it three working days after the deadline

MTD sign-up

Automatic when you register for VAT, unless you’re exempt

Digital links

Mandatory since April 2021 (no copying and pasting between records)

Late submission penalties

Points-based system since 1 January 2023. The late return that takes you to your threshold triggers a £200 penalty, and further late returns while you’re at the threshold can trigger further £200 penalties

Late payment penalties

From day 16 after the deadline, rising from day 31

How has Making Tax Digital been rolled out?

In stages: MTD for VAT started in April 2019 and has covered all VAT-registered businesses since April 2022, while MTD for Income Tax began in April 2026.

You should also view Sage’s MTD Hub to ensure you keep on top of key dates.

May 2015: The Chancellor announced the “death of the annual tax return” and impending digitalisation of VAT, Income Tax and Corporation Tax within five years. Therefore, Making Tax Digital is created and plans are made to start rolling it out.

December 2015: HMRC launched personal tax accounts, by which individual taxpayers can manage tax online, such as their PAYE codes and National Insurance records.

April 2019: Making Tax Digital for VAT came into effect. Most businesses over the VAT threshold had to begin following the rules for their first full VAT period after this date. MTD-compatible software must be used for filing VAT Returns, and relevant VAT accounting records must be kept digitally.

October 2019: MTD for VAT came into effect for businesses that were deferred in April 2019. This list mostly comprises larger businesses and organisations, such as group companies and public sector organisations.

April 2021: The soft landing period came to an end. Prior to this, it was possible for those using MTD for VAT to manually copy and paste data. But after this date, the movement of data from one place to another must be both automated and digital—something known as digital linking.

April 2022: MTD for VAT was extended to all VAT-registered businesses. This includes those that were voluntarily registered for VAT. The rules and requirements of MTD for VAT remain the same: for the first full VAT period following April 2022, any individual or business registered for VAT must use MTD-compatible software for filing VAT Returns, and relevant VAT accounting records must be kept digitally.

January 2023: A new penalty system applies to VAT late submissions under Making Tax Digital. Each late return earns a penalty point. The late return that takes a business to its points threshold triggers a £200 penalty, and further late returns while it’s at the threshold can trigger further £200 penalties.

July 2025: HMRC confirmed in its Transformation Roadmap that MTD for Corporation Tax won’t go ahead. Companies continue to file Corporation Tax returns under the current system.

April 2026: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax (also known as MTD for Income Tax Self Assessment) began for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 a year. It’s separate from MTD for VAT and has its own rules.

From April 2026 and April 2027: The late submission and late payment penalty system is applied to MTD for Income Tax customers in line with mandation. Extension to all other Self Assessment customers is planned, with the date to be confirmed. For those who joined in April 2026, late quarterly updates in the 2026/27 tax year don’t attract penalty points (the soft landing period).

April 2027: MTD for Income Tax is extended to those with qualifying income over £30,000 a year.

April 2028: MTD for Income Tax is extended to those with qualifying income over £20,000 a year.

No earlier than April 2028: MTD for Income Tax for general partnerships (date to be confirmed).

Will the government extend MTD for Income Tax to other individuals and businesses, such as those earning below £20,000?

Or those who use Self Assessment for other things, such as declaring interest on investments, or if they have salaries over £100,000?

It’s possible, but there have been no announcements, so there are no dates yet.

However, the experience of the rollout of MTD for VAT over several years indicates this may be likely.

When is your MTD for VAT Return due?

Under standard VAT accounting, one calendar month and seven days after the end of your VAT period. The Annual Accounting Scheme is different: your return is normally two months after the end of an accounting period of 4 to 12 months, or one month after the end of a period shorter than four months.

HMRC now signs up businesses for MTD for VAT automatically when they register for VAT, unless they’re exempt (GOV.UK). If you’re not sure you’re signed up, see how to sign up for MTD for VAT.

Once you’re signed up, make sure your software is authorised to connect to HMRC. Speak to the software vendor if you have any questions on this.

If you have an accountant who handles your VAT, they can file returns on your behalf. Just ask them.

But do remember that this doesn’t remove the requirement for you to keep relevant VAT records digitally.

Because you must file VAT Returns by one calendar month and seven days after the end of your VAT period, at the latest, the due dates follow a set pattern. For example, if you file quarterly:

VAT quarter ends

Return and payment due

31 March

7 May

30 June

7 August

30 September

7 November

31 December

7 February

Monthly filers follow the same rule, so a return for April is due by 7 June. If you pay by Direct Debit, HMRC collects the payment three working days after the deadline.

These dates apply to standard VAT accounting, where the return and payment deadlines usually coincide. If you use the Annual Accounting Scheme, you pay instalments during the year and a balancing payment with your return. Businesses in the Payments on Account scheme make interim payments on separate dates too.

If you’re new to MTD for VAT software, your next VAT Return will be the first you create with it.

But don’t worry, this is usually very straightforward.

What happens if you miss an MTD for VAT deadline?

You get a penalty point for each late return, and a £200 penalty once you reach your points threshold. Paying late brings separate late payment penalties and interest.

Your penalty points threshold depends on how often you file (GOV.UK):

How often you file

Points threshold

To reset your points to zero

Annually

2

File on time for 24 months, and send any returns outstanding from the previous 24 months

Quarterly

4

File on time for 12 months, and send any returns outstanding from the previous 24 months

Monthly

5

File on time for six months, and send any returns outstanding from the previous 24 months

The late return that takes you to your threshold triggers the first £200 penalty. Each further late return while you’re at the threshold can trigger another £200 penalty.

Points below the threshold expire after about two years (GOV.UK).

If you pay late, there’s no penalty if you pay, or agree a Time to Pay arrangement, within 15 days. After that, you pay 3% of what you owed at day 15, a further 3% of what you still owe at day 30, and then a daily penalty of 10% a year from day 31 (GOV.UK). Late payment interest also applies.

HMRC does not offer general extensions for MTD for VAT deadlines. If you have a reasonable excuse (such as serious illness or a system outage), you can appeal a penalty. Time to Pay arrangements can help with paying VAT, but they don’t extend filing deadlines.

It’s worth noting that some people can apply to HMRC to be digitally excluded. This means they won’t have to deal with Making Tax Digital.

However, this exclusion is only for exceptional circumstances, and you can’t just opt into it.

You need a very good reason, such as the fact that the remoteness of your location means you can’t access the internet, or your religious beliefs prohibit you from using a computer. See HMRC’s exemption guidance.

For more detail, read HMRC MTD penalties explained.

How can you make sure you meet every MTD for VAT deadline?

Work through this checklist before each VAT period ends.

Confirm your VAT accounting periods and filing frequency (monthly, quarterly, or annually).

Choose and set up MTD-compatible software, and authorise it to connect to HMRC.

Check that you’re signed up for MTD for VAT. HMRC signs up new VAT registrations automatically.

Ensure digital links exist between all parts of your VAT accounting records (no copying and pasting).

Schedule your VAT Return preparation to meet the one month and seven days submission deadline.

Keep track of your penalty points, and pay on time to avoid late payment penalties.

Keep your VAT records digitally for at least six years.

Final thoughts on MTD deadlines

Making Tax Digital has arguably had a difficult gestation, as the revised deadlines demonstrate.

But it’s transforming the way VAT-registered businesses handle their accounting for the better.

MTD gives you better insight into your accounting, so you can take control of cash flow and forecasting.

MTD for VAT deadlines: FAQs

			

			

	

Is Making Tax Digital just for VAT?

	

			

No. MTD for Income Tax began in April 2026 for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000, and extends to those over £30,000 in April 2027 and £20,000 in April 2028. MTD for Corporation Tax was planned, but HMRC cancelled it in July 2025.

Keep an eye on Sage’s MTD Hub for an up-to-date listing of all the current MTD deadlines.

		

	

	

Who needs to register for Making Tax Digital for VAT?

	

			

Since April 2022, virtually all individuals and businesses that are registered for VAT need to follow the MTD for VAT rules.

This includes those that are voluntarily registered for VAT. HMRC signs up new VAT registrations automatically, unless they’re exempt.

Prior to April 2022, only businesses that were over the VAT threshold needed to register for MTD for VAT (although voluntary registration was possible).

If you’re in any doubt, see the separate article about MTD thresholds.

		

	

	

What was the soft landing period for MTD for VAT?

	

			

Back in 2019, the government announced that it would let businesses keep using copy and paste to move data from one place to another without contravening the Making Tax Digital legislation.

Under the MTD legislation, this is not allowed. It states that the data must move both automatically and digitally. After all, that’s one of the reasons MTD was created.

The soft landing period ended in April 2021, and there are no signs that HMRC is going to allow a second soft landing period for businesses switching to MTD for VAT now.

Therefore, businesses starting using MTD for VAT now need to know the digital linking rules from day one.

		

	

	

Has Making Tax Digital for VAT been postponed?

	

			

No. Since April 2022, MTD for VAT has applied to all VAT-registered businesses.

MTD for Income Tax was postponed several times. It was first planned for 2018, then April 2023, then April 2024, before starting in April 2026.

		

	

	

Do I need to sign up for MTD for VAT?

	

			

Usually not, because HMRC now signs up businesses automatically when they register for VAT, and it has also signed up the remaining VAT-registered businesses. If your software fails, contact your software provider and HMRC as soon as you can. Businesses that are exempt from MTD file in a different way, and the final VAT Return after deregistration is normally submitted through the VAT online account. A late return may result in a penalty point, subject to some exclusions, and you can appeal if you have a reasonable excuse.

	

	

Do deadline dates differ by business type?

	

			

No. The deadline depends on your VAT period and filing frequency, not whether you’re a sole trader, partnership, or limited company. Under standard VAT accounting, returns are due one month and seven days after the VAT period ends. Under the Annual Accounting Scheme, the return is normally two months after the end of an accounting period of 4 to 12 months, or one month after the end of a period shorter than four months.
