VAT groups generally have to follow Making Tax Digital (MTD) for VAT, as single businesses do, subject to exemptions and different final-return processes. The representative member must make sure the group’s VAT records are kept digitally, use digital links where relevant data moves between products, and file one VAT Return for the whole group using MTD-compatible software.

Key takeaways

VAT groups generally have to follow MTD for VAT, as single VAT-registered businesses do, subject to exemptions and different final-return processes.

The representative member keeps the group’s VAT records digitally and files one VAT Return for all members.

Required records can sit across different systems. Where relevant data moves between the products in the group’s software arrangement, it must move through digital links. Copying and pasting isn’t allowed.

VAT groups above the then £85,000 VAT threshold were deferred to VAT periods starting on or after 1 October 2019. MTD for VAT was extended to all VAT-registered businesses, including smaller groups, from April 2022.

All group members are jointly and severally liable for the group’s VAT debts.

Making Tax Digital for VAT has been around since April 2019.

Any individual or business registered for VAT must keep key VAT accounting records digitally and use software to submit their VAT Returns.

Effectively, this has meant most businesses use software for their accounting.

This brings benefits of its own, such as far better insights into business finances compared to attempting to keep accounting records manually.

MTD for VAT applies to VAT groups too, and brings the same rules and requirements.

This article explains how, and looks back at the deadlines that applied to VAT groups.

For more information about all aspects of Making Tax Digital, please visit Sage’s MTD hub.

Here’s what this article discusses:

How does Making Tax Digital apply to VAT groups?

In the same way as to a single business: the group files one VAT Return through MTD-compatible software, with digital links wherever relevant VAT data moves between the products it uses.

So, what is a VAT group?

Sometimes it’s financially sensible for two or more companies (known as bodies corporate), or a company together with the individuals or partnerships that control it, to use just one VAT registration (VAT Notice 700/2).

This is known as a VAT group registration.

In practical terms, it means one member of the group acts as the representative member for VAT purposes. This member is responsible for VAT Returns, plus paying and reclaiming VAT, for all the members of the group.

Here’s how a VAT group works (VAT Notice 700/2):

 

VAT group

Who can join

Two or more UK-established companies under common control, plus any individuals or partnerships that control a company in the group

Who files the VAT Return

The representative member, on behalf of the whole group

Supplies between members

Usually disregarded for VAT, with some exceptions for services

Who is liable for VAT debts

All members, jointly and severally

How to apply

Online, uploading form VAT50/51 as part of the application

MTD for VAT

Applies in full: digital records, digital links, and MTD-compatible software

Another key benefit is that members of the VAT group usually don’t need to account for VAT when making supplies to each other.

How much input tax the group can recover depends on how the group as a whole uses its purchases, and on the supplies it makes outside the group. Partial exemption and other rules may restrict recovery, so check VAT Notice 700/2 and VAT Notice 706.

Group VAT registrations generally have to follow Making Tax Digital for VAT, just like any individual VAT-registered business, subject to exemptions and different final-return processes.

But things are much more complex with VAT groups compared to a standalone VAT business, because there’s typically a lot more data to be gathered for each return.

This might exist in several locations.

Under the rules of MTD for VAT, the required VAT records may sit across several systems in the group. Where relevant electronic data moves between the products that make up the group’s compatible-software arrangement, it must move through digital links.

That data is then used to prepare the VAT Return.

It’s because of issues such as this that HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) allowed several delays for larger organisations such as VAT groups following the start of Making Tax Digital for VAT in April 2019.

When did MTD for VAT start for VAT groups?

VAT groups in the original mandation scope, with taxable turnover above the then £85,000 threshold, were deferred to VAT periods starting on or after 1 October 2019. Groups below that threshold came into MTD for VAT from their first VAT period starting on or after 1 April 2022. For groups already in MTD, the digital links soft landing ended for VAT periods starting on or after 1 April 2021; groups joining from April 2022 needed digital links from the start.

Although now passed, there were two key deadlines for Making Tax Digital for VAT when it comes to VAT groups. To stay up to date on the latest deadlines, be sure to visit Sage’s MTD hub, which is updated regularly. For current dates, see Making Tax Digital for VAT deadlines.

October 2019

This was the deadline by which VAT groups needed to start observing the rules of MTD for VAT.

In other words, it applied for the first full VAT accounting period after October 2019.

This meant that, if the VAT group filed quarterly VAT Returns, and their first MTD for VAT period started in October 2019, the first MTD for VAT Return would have needed to have been submitted in early February 2020.

Larger organisations such as VAT groups got this extension following the April 2019 introduction date because of the typical complexity of their systems, and likely issues arising in getting everything ready in time.

April 2021

When Making Tax Digital for VAT started, HMRC allowed what was known as the soft landing period.

Businesses could ignore a key part of the digital linking requirement—namely, that manually copying or cutting and pasting data between two locations was prohibited.

As mentioned, when it comes to VAT group registrations, creating a VAT Return can involve collating information from various sources. Therefore, being able to cut, copy, and paste is very useful.

HMRC originally planned for the full digital linking rules to apply to VAT groups from October 2020. Because of the coronavirus pandemic, it extended the soft landing period for all businesses to their first VAT period starting on or after 1 April 2021 (ICAEW).

This meant cutting, copying, and pasting was against the law when it came to key VAT accounting data and preparing the VAT Return. Any businesses caught doing so could be penalised by HMRC.

For those filing group VAT Returns, this came as something of a blow—but HMRC had given group VAT members until April 2021 to prepare.

What are digital links, and how do they work in a VAT group?

They’re automated ways of moving data between software, such as an export and import, so nobody retypes or copies and pastes VAT data.

The rules of Making Tax Digital say the relevant accounting data must be stored digitally.

Furthermore, software must be used to send returns or other kinds of updates to HMRC, as required within the MTD rules.

Therefore, if you use more than one piece of software or more than one system, any transfer of relevant VAT data between them must be through a digital link.

It must be possible to automatically transfer the data from one digital location to another.

You might have to click a button to start off this automated transfer, but the key thing is that you’re not doing it manually—perhaps by copying and pasting the data, or even scribbling it into a notebook and then rekeying it into another system.

That said, what’s considered digital linking can sometimes be surprising and a little counterintuitive. Emailing a spreadsheet is fine. You can even pass data to somebody via USB memory stick.

For example, HMRC describes a VAT group where each member exports a monthly summary from its own software into a master spreadsheet, which then connects to HMRC through bridging software (VAT Notice 700/22).

The rules for digital linking for Making Tax Digital for VAT can be found in the VAT Notice 700/22.

MTD for Income Tax, which began in April 2026, has its own digital record-keeping rules. MTD for Corporation Tax was cancelled in July 2025.

Final thoughts on MTD for VAT groups

VAT groups offer a useful way to account for VAT across several businesses.

It can reduce complexity and costs.

But it also brings its own requirements when it comes to legally complying with MTD for VAT’s requirements, and particularly the ban on copying, cutting, and pasting data from one place to another.

However, the benefits of using Making Tax Digital for VAT—and therefore using software for VAT Return submissions—outweigh this extra work.

MTD for VAT groups: FAQs

			

			

	

What is a VAT group?

	

			

A VAT group is a single VAT registration covering two or more companies you control, so you submit one VAT Return reporting all the group members’ supplies and acquisitions. Supplies between group members are usually disregarded for VAT.

However, there are some exceptions to this, including some bought-in services, and the cost component for some supplies. This is detailed in Section 7 of VAT Notice 700/2.

There are also certain limitations on what entities can form VAT groups. These are listed in Section 2.2 of VAT Notice 700/2.

		

	

	

Who can form a VAT group?

	

			

Bodies corporate (limited companies, public limited companies, and so on) that are established or have a fixed establishment in the UK, and are under common control. Individuals, partnerships, and Scottish partnerships can join too, but only if they control a UK company in the group. Non-corporate bodies have been able to join since 1 November 2019.

	

	

What is a VAT group registration?

	

			

A single VAT registration covering all members of a VAT group. The group is treated as one taxable person, and the representative member files one VAT Return on behalf of all members. To apply, you complete form VAT50/51 and upload it as part of your online VAT registration application.

	

	

How do I submit a group VAT Return?

	

			

Submitting a group VAT Return is done just like it is for an individual or business. You need to use software to submit the VAT Return, as per the rules of MTD for VAT.

The software connects to HMRC’s computers across the internet so you can file the VAT Return.

A spreadsheet can be used to compile VAT accounting data for a group VAT Return, provided the digital linking rules above are not broken.

Bridging software can then be used with the spreadsheet to make a VAT Return submission to HMRC.

However, most VAT groups use MTD-compatible software for their VAT accounting, and so are easily able to create the VAT Return based on data already within the system(s).

For step-by-step guidance, see Making Tax Digital for VAT: complete guide.

		

	

	

Are VAT group members liable for each other’s VAT?

	

			

Yes. All members of a VAT group are jointly and severally liable for any VAT the group owes, even though the representative member files the return (VAT Notice 700/2).

title: How to get ready for Making Tax Digital for VAT
snippet: You don't usually need to sign up for Making Tax Digital for VAT. Find out how it applies, what software you need, and how to keep digital records and file VAT Returns. The post How to get ready for Making Tax Digital for VAT appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Making Tax Digital (MTD) for VAT requires VAT-registered businesses to keep prescribed VAT records digitally and to file VAT Returns through compatible software. You don’t usually need to sign up yourself. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) automatically signs up newly VAT-registered businesses unless they’re exempt or awaiting an exemption decision.

Key takeaways

You don’t usually need to sign up for MTD for VAT. HMRC signs up newly VAT-registered businesses automatically, unless they’re exempt or waiting for an exemption decision.

It applies to every VAT-registered business, including those that registered voluntarily below the £90,000 threshold (since 1 April 2024).

What you do need is compatible software, with your VAT records kept digitally. Spreadsheets are fine if bridging software links them to HMRC.

Your HMRC online VAT account can’t be used to send your regular VAT Returns any more. The final return after you deregister is normally the exception.

A small number of businesses are exempt, some automatically. Others can apply by phone or in writing if using digital tools isn’t practical for them.

This article covers the main MTD for VAT rules for UK businesses. Different rules can apply to businesses in Northern Ireland, overseas businesses, VAT groups, insolvency cases, and special VAT schemes, so check HMRC’s MTD for VAT guidance if any of these apply to you.

Here’s what this article discusses:

Making Tax Digital for VAT started in April 2019 for VAT-registered businesses over the VAT threshold.

Since April 2022, MTD for VAT has applied to all VAT-registered businesses, including businesses that are voluntarily registered and under the threshold.

They must store their VAT accounting records digitally and use compatible software for their VAT accounting.

Compatible software may help streamline some VAT record-keeping and submission processes, depending on your existing systems and how the software is configured.

Do I need to sign up for Making Tax Digital for VAT?

Usually not, because all VAT-registered businesses should now be signed up for MTD for VAT unless they’re exempt or awaiting an exemption decision, and HMRC automatically signs up newly VAT-registered businesses.

You can no longer use your HMRC online VAT account to send monthly or quarterly VAT Returns—you need to file through compatible software. You may still use your online account for other VAT tasks, and the final VAT Return after you cancel your registration is normally submitted there.

Penalties depend on the specific failure and your circumstances. Late VAT Returns earn penalty points, as the FAQs below explain. It’s your responsibility to make sure your records and returns meet the MTD rules.

How do I get ready for Making Tax Digital for VAT?

Here’s how to get your business ready for MTD for VAT:

Confirm your VAT registration: check your VAT registration number and the effective date of registration shown by HMRC.

Choose compatible software: choose compatible record-keeping or bridging software before your next VAT Return is due. This can be a single accounting package, or bridging software that connects suitable digital records, such as spreadsheets, to HMRC. See Find software that’s compatible with Making Tax Digital for VAT.

Authorise your software: follow your software provider’s instructions to authorise it to interact with HMRC. You’ll usually need your Government Gateway user ID and password.

Keep your records digitally: keep the prescribed VAT records digitally. If you use more than one software product, transfers of data between them generally need to be made through digital links. VAT Notice 700/22 sets out the rules.

File your VAT Returns through your software: submit each VAT Return through your compatible software by its deadline. You can use accounting software to submit your VAT Return to HMRC.

Should I register for VAT voluntarily?

There are two separate tests for compulsory VAT registration. You have to register if your taxable turnover for the previous 12 months is more than £90,000 (threshold accurate as of 1 April 2024), checked at the end of each month on a rolling basis. You also have to register if you expect your taxable turnover in the next 30 days alone to be more than £90,000. Taxable turnover includes zero-rated sales as well as standard-rated and reduced-rated ones, but not exempt sales or sales outside the scope of VAT. See VAT thresholds.

Below that, registering is your choice.

The main reason businesses register voluntarily is to reclaim VAT on their costs. You can usually reclaim VAT on things you buy for your business, as long as you have valid VAT invoices. Some costs can’t be reclaimed—business entertainment is a common example—and there are extra rules if you make both taxable and exempt sales. You may also be able to reclaim VAT on some costs from before you registered, but only within time limits. HMRC’s VAT Input Tax manual has the detail.

The trade-off is that you’ll need to charge VAT on your taxable sales, file VAT Returns, and follow the MTD for VAT rules, which can affect your prices and cash flow. It’s worth talking it through with an accountant or tax adviser before you decide.

You can register for VAT online, or your accountant can do it for you. If you’re doing it yourself, you’ll need a Government Gateway account for your business.

Once you’re registered, HMRC sends your VAT number and confirms your effective date of registration. You account for VAT from that date, which depends on why you registered (or the date you agreed for a voluntary registration) and can be earlier than the day your number arrives. See Register for VAT. Quote your VAT number on your VAT invoices.

Can my accountant handle MTD for VAT for me?

Yes, your accountant can handle MTD for VAT if they’re authorised to act for you. An authorised agent can handle tasks such as setting up software and filing VAT Returns on your behalf.

Handing over the admin doesn’t hand over responsibility, though. It’s still down to you to keep accurate digital records and to make sure the returns submitted for you are right.

Your accountant may ask that you link your accounting software with theirs.

Can I be exempt from Making Tax Digital for VAT?

Most VAT-registered businesses must follow MTD for VAT. Some are automatically exempt, while others may apply where using computers, software, or the internet is not reasonable or practical.

Some businesses have genuine reasons why they’re unable to comply with Making Tax Digital. These include the following:

Reasons of age, disability, remoteness of location or, in HMRC’s words, “any other reason” that means it’s not “reasonably practicable” for the business owner to use digital tools to keep business records or submit returns. For example, a business without an internet connection because it’s on an island that’s off the grid might be considered exempt.

Religious beliefs are incompatible with the requirements of MTD for VAT. This is typically that the individuals running the business are unable to use computers because of their beliefs.

Apply by calling or writing to HMRC. Continue to send returns in your usual way until HMRC issues its decision. See Apply for an exemption from Making Tax Digital for VAT.

It’s important to note that if HMRC believes exemption isn’t appropriate, it may offer digital assistance to help your business get online support.

Can I cancel my VAT registration to avoid MTD for VAT?

You may be able to ask HMRC to cancel your registration if HMRC is satisfied that your taxable turnover in the relevant future period will not exceed £88,000 (threshold accurate as of 1 April 2024). Separate rules can apply, including to businesses based outside the UK.

VAT registration can be cancelled online, or you can fill in and then post a VAT7 form to HMRC.

HMRC says it will usually contact you within 40 working days, although it may take longer during busy periods.

HMRC will confirm the effective cancellation date. The date depends on why the registration is being cancelled and may not be the date of the request.

Up to that date, you should continue to observe VAT requirements.

You’ll need to submit a final VAT Return for the period up to the cancellation date. This final return is normally submitted through your VAT online account, not through MTD software. Different routes can apply if your business is exempt from MTD or is in insolvency, so check HMRC’s guidance.

You may have to account for VAT on stock and assets you still have at the cancellation date, depending on how you acquired them and how VAT was treated at the time (for example, whether you reclaimed VAT when you bought them). You don’t have to pay this VAT if the total due is £1,000 or less.

The rules can be technical, and special cases such as assets transferred with a business, land, and capital items have their own rules, so check VAT Notice 700/11 or speak to your accountant.

What if my software won’t connect to HMRC?

Software usually fails to connect because your details don’t match HMRC’s records, its authorisation has lapsed, or your accountant isn’t authorised to act for you.

Your details don’t match HMRC’s records: this can happen if your business name or address has changed since you registered. Double-check your VAT number, business name, and address exactly as HMRC holds them.

Your software isn’t authorised for MTD: authorisation can lapse, for example if you’ve switched software or it’s been a while since you connected. Follow your provider’s instructions to reconnect it to HMRC.

Your accountant can’t see your VAT account: check they’re authorised to act for you for MTD for VAT in their Agent Services Account.

MTD for VAT readiness checklist

Work through this before your next VAT Return is due. If you’re already filing through software, you’ve probably ticked off most of it.

Confirm you’re VAT-registered, and check your VAT number and effective date of registration

Choose compatible accounting or bridging software

Have your Government Gateway user ID and password to hand

Authorise your software to interact with HMRC

Keep your VAT records digitally, using digital links between any software products

If you use an accountant, make sure they’re authorised to act for you

File each VAT Return through your software by its deadline

Final thoughts on MTD for VAT

Now you know how MTD for VAT works and what you need to do, you can get your business ready.

If you’re not sure where to start, work through the readiness checklist above, then fill in any gaps.

Need more help with MTD for VAT?

Speak to your accountant about the requirements—they can help you examine processes in your business to see what needs to be adapted. Alternatively, visit the dedicated MTD hub for more information.

Signing up for Making Tax Digital for VAT FAQs

			

			

	

How do I sign up for Making Tax Digital for VAT?

	

			

Use HMRC’s MTD sign up service, then activate MTD in your compatible software before filing.

	

	

Does MTD for VAT apply if I’m below the VAT threshold?

	

			

Yes, MTD for VAT applies below the threshold if you’re VAT-registered. Since April 2022 the rules have covered every VAT-registered business, including those that registered voluntarily, whatever their turnover.

	

	

Can I still send VAT Returns through my HMRC online account?

	

			

You can’t send monthly or quarterly VAT Returns through your online account—those have to go through compatible software. Your online account still works for other VAT tasks, and the final VAT Return after deregistration is normally submitted there.

	

	

What happens if I send a VAT Return late?

	

			

You get a penalty point for each late return. Quarterly filers get a £200 penalty when they reach four points, and another £200 for each late return after that. This points-based system has applied to VAT since January 2023. Read more in Making Tax Digital for Income Tax penalties: HMRC’s new systems explained, which covers VAT too.

	

	

Can I be exempt from MTD for VAT?

	

			

Possibly. Some businesses are exempt automatically. Others can apply if using computers, software, or the internet isn’t practical for them—because of age, disability, where they’re based, or religious beliefs, for example. Call or write to HMRC to apply, and keep filing as normal while you wait for a decision.

title: Embedded accounting: The opportunity for accountants
snippet: As clients change how they keep their books, discover what embedded accounting means for your role and your practice. The post Embedded accounting: The opportunity for accountants appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
More small businesses are now recording income and expenses directly in the banking and business apps they use every day.

But that doesn’t remove the need for professional accounting advice.

In fact, it can create new opportunities to support clients, particularly those who are still building confidence with digital record-keeping.

Clients still need your expertise to assess what they’ve recorded, identify what’s missing, and understand what it means for their business.

This article breaks down what embedded accounting means for your practice, how to support clients using it and take advantage of its benefits, and how Sage is helping accountants and bookkeepers stay connected to the record.

Here’s what we’ll cover:

What is embedded accounting?

Embedded accounting means accounting features are built directly into the banking, fintech, and business software platforms your clients already use.

This could look like capturing receipts, categorising transactions, or creating invoices within the same app they use to manage their money, depending on their chosen platform.

Many small businesses want to manage more of their day-to-day administration from a single platform.

Embedded accounting responds to that need by bringing record-keeping into the places where they already manage business activity.

What embedded accounting could mean for your practice?

You know how much time it takes chasing receipts or getting a clear explanation from a client about a payment they made months ago.

Embedded accounting helps clients build cleaner, digitised records from day one, giving you a better starting point for review.

Capturing information as they go also helps establish healthy digital habits, with Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax readiness built into the process from the start.

That can mean less chasing at quarter or year-end, when clients may have forgotten the details.

Being able to review those records without learning a different process for every client’s app is another big benefit.

A consistent workflow gives you new visibility into what clients have recorded and a way to address errors or missing information.

Clients can handle everyday record-keeping while you retain the professional oversight they rely on.

Embedded accounting also creates an opportunity for you to support new clients through the platforms they already use.

Small businesses can be more comfortable keeping everyday records in their existing apps but still need an accountant’s help.

You can build a relationship around the support they need now and develop it as their businesses grow.

How to support clients already using embedded accounting

Your clients may not call it “embedded accounting.” 

Instead, they may tell you they have already categorised transactions or uploaded receipts in their banking app. 

Start by asking which platform they use and how they’ve been using it.

That should give you an idea of what information is available and the support they may need.

Next, establish your access to their records.

You’ll need to agree on the appropriate permissions with your client and understand where their platform supports accountant access, or a connection to the tools you use.

Confirm what information is shared and whether amendments update the underlying client record, so you both understand how you will work together.

Then consider what the app hasn’t captured.

Has the client used other accounts or cards? Have they paid business expenses personally?

Are there cash payments? These questions help you establish whether the records reflect the wider business activity.

Reviewing the records brings it all together.

For the period you are reviewing, check that transactions are supported, categorisation is appropriate, and gaps have been addressed.

For example, a payment labelled as a business expense may need clarification about what was purchased and how it was used before you can make the correct adjustments.

Set a regular cadence for resolving queries with your client.

Get clear about responsibilities for supplying information, reviewing entries, and handling submission to keep the work moving throughout the year.

How Sage keeps accountants connected to the record

Sage’s role in the embedded accounting evolution is to connect the place your embedded accounting clients keep their records with the tools you use to support them. 

Sage for Accountants’ Period Review capability provides accountants with a single, unified workflow for reviewing client data and preparing records before filing.

It connects your review work to the records your client maintains in their connected partner app.

You can search, sort, and update records in bulk within one consistent review experience, whether records come from Sage ledgers or Sage’s embedded accounting partner apps.

Supported by Sage-backed accounting standards, this helps you improve data quality throughout the year and build confidence that records are ready for submission.

Even if you don’t use the full version of Sage for Accountants today, you can still support clients using embedded accounting and plug directly into their activity.

Sage’s Period Review is now available for free within the software.

You can leverage the same visibility, review, and correct records with speed, all without learning a new workflow or app for every client. Sage Period Review for Accountants was built for accountants, by accountants.

The connection and functionality available will vary depending on the platform your client uses.

You can access Period Review through Sage for Accountants.

Get started today

If your practice isn’t already using Sage for Accountants, it’s easy to sign up and get started, so you can start making Period Review part of the way you work.

A new start to a deeper connection

Embedded accounting allows your clients to keep the freedom of choosing the products that suit them without changing where they start.

Sage for Accountants keeps you connected to their records, so you can support them as their business develops.

And there will be opportunities to do more.

 Future integrations will mean more tools and capabilities as Sage continues to partner with more of the platforms your current and potential clients use to manage their money.

title: Beyond the brief: Where do accountants’ hidden hours go?
snippet: Providing business-critical advice, reassurance and answering unexpected client questions all take time. Discover what The Hidden Hours of Accountancy conversation reveals about accountants’ changing workload, and how practices can make that work more visible. The post Beyond the brief: Where do accountants’ hidden hours go? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Accountants’ hidden hours include the advice, reassurance and coordination surrounding their core services.

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research from Sage found that 81% of accountants work outside their scope, highlighting how widely support extends beyond the agreed brief.

Accountants can discuss current figures with clients without waiting for records to arrive. But both sides need to agree who keeps those records up to date and when the accountant will review them.

Technology can save processing time while introducing demands around learning, client support and ongoing oversight.

Recognising recurring extra work helps practices plan their services, improve workflows and set clearer expectations.

Ask an accountant what they’d do with five extra hours a week, and the answer can be surprisingly personal.

“I’d probably stop working on a Saturday,” said Andrew Dick, owner of G W Dick & Co.

His answer points to a pattern many accountants and bookkeepers will recognise, and it’s what we discuss in this article, as follows:

Alongside the agreed work sits another layer: the client question that turns into a conversation about the future of the business, the reassurance before a big decision, the software problem that lands in your inbox. 

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research from Sage found that 81% of respondents work outside their scope.

In the first The Hidden Hours of Accountancy episode, which you can watch above, Andrew and Julie Young, managing directors of Walter Dawson & Son Accountants, explore where that time goes. They go on to explain why the support that makes a client relationship valuable can also make the workload harder to contain.

Accountants’ hidden hours are the time spent on work surrounding their core services, some of which goes unbilled. That can include chasing information, explaining requirements, answering unexpected questions, helping clients navigate software and providing reassurance when a business decision feels difficult.

Some of this work is necessary to complete an agreed task. Some develops as clients bring more of their concerns to someone they trust. During a busy day, there may be little opportunity to consider how each request fits into the service being paid for.

In the video above, Andrew describes how closely business and personal concerns overlap for small business owners. A problem in the business affects life at home, while a family issue can influence what happens at work. An accountant may become the first person a client approaches because they already understand the business and its history.

Julie describes a similar instinct to help. Asking more questions and understanding what a client wants to achieve can reveal what they actually need from their accountant.

These conversations have professional value. They can lead to better advice and a clearer understanding of the client’s goals. The difficulty is accounting for the time they take and the responsibility they create. When the work stays hidden, it becomes easy to underestimate the time and capacity it really takes to serve its clients well.

How client support grows beyond the brief

Additional support often grows through ordinary interactions. A client asks a question, their accountant helps, and the client gains confidence in them.

Over time, this can become a continuous relationship. Clients want to discuss decisions while they still have options, and accountants have an opportunity to help before a commitment has been made.

Julie’s discussion of ongoing client relationships shows why this matters. Understanding what a client is considering gives an accountant more room to offer useful advice than discovering the decision later in the records.

But the same willingness to help can make it difficult to recognise when the service has expanded. Julie acknowledges that accountants can give valuable support away because they care about their clients and want to solve the problem in front of them.

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research found that 70% of accountants said their fees do not reflect the support they provide. Alongside Julie’s experience, that finding raises a question about how clearly the full service is understood and recognised.

The client experiences a helpful answer. The accountant fits another conversation between existing commitments. Neither necessarily pauses to discuss whether this is an occasional request or the start of an ongoing need.

Across a client base, those decisions add up. What looks like a manageable favour in isolation can become a regular part of the working week.

The same pattern showed up at Accountex Summit Manchester. Ask the Accountant podcast host Aaron Patrick described how the first Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax quarterly update exposed work his practice had underestimated.

Having participated in the beta programme since 2022, he was confident about filing. Getting clients signed up, receiving their data on time and helping them understand the change proved more challenging.

“I had to completely and utterly rip up my capacity planning,” he said.

For the next stage, his practice was bringing engagement letters forward and setting clearer expectations about fees and what clients needed to provide. Aaron also recognised that repeated communication from his practice did not mean every client understood the change: some were still hearing about it for the first time.

His experience shows why the conversations around a service need space in the plan. Explaining the change, agreeing responsibilities and getting clients ready all take time before the submission itself.

Making that surrounding work visible gives both sides a better basis for discussing the service. Clients can understand what is involved, while practices can plan for the support surrounding the task as well as the task itself.

Why technology changes where the time goes

Technology can make information available sooner and reduce the effort required for individual tasks. It also changes what accountants need to understand and what clients may expect them to do.

Julie describes earlier access to client records as an important change in the profession. When information is available throughout the year, accountants can use it to support decisions closer to the moment they are being made.

That creates opportunities for more timely conversations. Instead of waiting for a client to bring in records, an accountant can work with information already available in the software.

In episode one of The Hidden Hours of Accountancy video series, Andrew highlights the learning involved. Accountants may need to understand several platforms, keep up with changes and help clients work through unfamiliar processes.

A practice can therefore become faster at processing information while spending more time on the activities around it. Looking only at the time technology saves on one task can miss where the work has moved across the rest of the working week.

Continuous access also raises questions about responsibility. Andrew points out that boundaries can become less clear when an accountant can see into a client’s software throughout the year.

A client may assume that someone is watching for problems. Their accountant may expect to review the records at agreed points. Both can believe the other is taking care of something unless the arrangement is made explicit.

Who maintains the records? Who checks them, and how often? What should prompt the client to get in touch?

Answering those questions helps turn shared access into a workable service. It also makes the limits of that service easier to understand.

A useful starting point is to look at what happens during a normal working week.

Which questions recur? Where do you repeatedly chase information? What software problems do clients bring to you? Which conversations regularly grow beyond the original request?

Recording those patterns can help a practice see where its capacity goes. It can also distinguish valuable support that deserves a clearer place in the service from avoidable administration.

1. Recognise recurring support

If the same kind of request keeps appearing, it may reflect an ongoing client need.

A regular planning conversation, clearer guidance or a defined support arrangement could serve the client better than a series of urgent requests. Recognising the pattern gives you something specific to discuss.

The aim is to understand how the relationship has developed and whether the service still fits.

2. Agree who does what

Where records and software are shared, explain responsibilities in practical terms.

Clients need to know what information they should maintain, what you will review and when they should raise a concern. Clear expectations can reduce uncertainty and give both sides more confidence in the arrangement.

These conversations are particularly useful when introducing software or changing a working process, because familiar assumptions may no longer apply.

3. Review the steps around the task

Look at the process as well as the final activity. Repeated requests for information, disconnected systems and unclear handovers can all add effort.

Aaron described how his practice was using embedded accounting with clients working in Tide.

His clients categorised payments in their banking app, with those categories coming through to his accounting system for review. This allowed them to contribute information through a tool they already used, while the practice retained the work of checking and correcting it.

For Aaron, the appeal was reducing friction in the client relationship. His example also provides a useful way to assess a connected workflow: does it make information easier to provide and review, and is it clear where the accountant’s attention and judgement are still needed?

4. Make room for judgement

Some conversations need time. Understanding a business owner’s ambitions or helping them think through a difficult decision can be central to good advice.

Making this work visible helps a practice decide how to accommodate it. It creates a firmer basis for planning capacity and discussing the service when a client’s needs change.

What would five hours back make possible?

Towards the end of the episode, the conversation turns to what getting five hours back would mean.

The question brings the discussion back to the people doing the work. Time saved has value because of what it makes possible, whether that is a more considered client conversation, space to work on the practice or an evening with fewer unfinished tasks on your mind.

The Hidden Hours of Accountancy research found that 77% of accountants struggle to switch off. That gives the discussion of capacity a personal consequence. How work is organised can affect what people carry beyond the end of the working day.

Julie would invest some of the time in thinking about her own business and how to move it forward. Helping clients can absorb so much attention that there is little space left to consider the practice’s own goals.

Their answers reveal two things hidden hours can displace: time away from work and time to plan its future. For Andrew, getting time back would mean a Saturday away from work. For Julie, it would mean space to plan the future of her own practice—the kind of thinking she helps clients do for theirs.

Final thoughts

Start with your own last working week. Identify one recurring piece of work that has grown beyond the agreed service. Is it support that needs a clearer place, an expectation that needs discussing or a process that could work better?

Use that example to begin a conversation with your team or client about what should change.

Getting time back starts with understanding where it is going. Making hidden work visible gives you the opportunity to decide what should be valued, redesigned or simply done differently.

Frequently asked questions

			

			

	

How can accountants spot scope creep early?

	

			

Look for repeated requests extending beyond the agreed service, such as ongoing software support, additional analysis or frequent advice on new decisions. Consider their cumulative effect on time and responsibility. A recurring pattern provides a basis for discussing the client’s changing needs.

	

	

Does access to client software mean an accountant is monitoring it continuously?

	

			

Access alone does not establish a review schedule. Clients and accountants should agree who maintains information, how often reviews happen and which issues the client needs to raise. Those expectations should be reflected clearly in the service arrangement.

	

	

How can accountants explain additional work to clients?

	

			

Describe the work in specific terms and connect it to the client’s needs. Explain how the requests relate to the existing service, then discuss an arrangement that supports them going forward. Using concrete examples makes the conversation easier to understand and plan around.

fullText:
Switching your practice from Self Assessment to Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax means moving from one annual tax return to year-round digital records, quarterly updates, and a digital tax return, for every client above the MTD threshold. Because the threshold falls from £50,000 to £30,000 in April 2027 and £20,000 in April 2028, most practices will run both systems side by side for several years.

Key takeaways

MTD for Income Tax makes tax a continuous, year-round process rather than a year-end project.

Practices will run Self Assessment and MTD side by side until at least April 2028, as the threshold falls to £30,000 and then £20,000.

Support clients in the way they prefer to work: do it for me, do it with me, or show me.

Build a digital record-keeping stack that suits each client. Suitable spreadsheets used with compatible bridging software can remain a compliant option.

Client management software and agentic AI can take on routine admin, so your team can focus on reviewing data and advising clients.

The era of MTD for Income Tax is upon us. But Self Assessment isn’t going away anytime soon.

The goal moving forward for practices is to find a way to support all sole traders and landlords, regardless of which HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) path they’re following—while also supporting client growth.

Practices need to find a way to somehow deliver what clients require: from a light touch, collaborative approach for those more confident in business finances, to a full-service offering for those who have traditionally relied heavily upon their accountant. Even in the MTD era, the latter is still entirely possible—and still desired by some clients, of course.

This article explains how to provide that support.

Here’s what this article discusses:

How should you redesign your practice workflows for MTD for Income Tax?

Redesign your workflows to be digital-first and continuous: MTD for Income Tax turns tax from a year-end project into a year-round process. The change is technology-driven.

Not only is the clue right there in the title with MTD—it’s about digitalising tax, after all—but applied and smart use of technology is the only way accountants and bookkeepers are going to get through without serious stress.

This means deploying the right software and going digital-first to transition from Self Assessment to MTD as the decade progresses—and as the April 2027 and April 2028 milestones approach (and possibly beyond).

To identify which clients are in scope, check each client’s Self Assessment position and their combined gross income from self-employment and property, before expenses, on the relevant earlier return: more than £50,000 on the 2024/25 return for April 2026, more than £30,000 on the 2025/26 return for April 2027, and more than £20,000 on the 2026/27 return for April 2028. Then check whether any exemptions apply.

Meanwhile, as an accountant, you’ll also have to help many of your clients along the same journey. Their success is your success. Their growth is your growth.

Your overarching digital strategy needs to be able to deliver for the “do-it-with-me” clients, who need a partner, and a full service “do-it-for-me” approach for clients who need that, too. 

Others will prefer support based on “show me”, in which you’ll offer them guidance but, essentially, they’ll do the majority of work themselves.

Most practices will need to offer all three:

Support model

Who it suits

What you provide

Do it for me

Clients who have always relied on their accountant

A full service: you maintain records and submit quarterly updates. For the annual return, as main agent you check it, share it with the client, and get their written confirmation before you submit it

Do it with me

Clients who want a partner

Shared software and regular collaboration through the year

Show me

Clients confident with their finances

Guidance and checks, while they do most of the work themselves

To price each model, read Pricing for MTD: How to charge more, and prove it’s worth it.

You need to support MTD’s quarterly check-ins, bearing in mind these can (and maybe should) be more frequent if clients desire it. You need to support the MTD tax return, as well as traditional yearly tax return checkpoints for Self Assessment happening at the same time. All while meeting ongoing quarterly and monthly VAT deadlines, of course.

The fundamental truth is this: MTD for Income Tax shifts accountancy to a continuous process rather than one that leads up to the final end of year calculations. This is a monumental shift, and it needs to form the basis of any changes.

Here’s how the two systems compare:

 

Self Assessment

MTD for Income Tax

Who it applies to

Sole traders and landlords below the MTD threshold, and other Self Assessment taxpayers

Individuals in Self Assessment whose combined gross self-employment and property income on the relevant earlier return is more than £50,000 (from April 2026), £30,000 (from April 2027), or £20,000 (from April 2028), unless exempt

Records

Can be kept on paper or spreadsheets

Must be kept digitally in MTD-compatible software, with digital links

Submissions

One tax return a year

Four quarterly updates, plus a digital tax return

Deadlines

31 January after the tax year

Quarterly updates by 7 August, 7 November, 7 February, and 7 May; tax return by 31 January

Practice workflow

Work peaks before 31 January

Continuous, with a checkpoint every quarter

For the quarterly process, read MTD quarterly updates: A practice guide for accountants and bookkeepers.

Whatever support your clients require, you should already be redesigning your own procedures and workflows, your data processing, and the way you interact with your clients to make them all digital-first.

How can technology cut reconciliation work under MTD?

Technology can cut reconciliation work by suggesting matches and flagging exceptions, although your team still needs to reconcile, check for missing information, confirm tax categories, and review the results.

Technology increasingly allows for light-touch reconciliations.

Whereas under the old systems, you would typically review and match every item manually, many matches can now be suggested automatically for your team to check.

This is particularly true for your clients whose businesses include high transaction volumes and those who produce simple, clear, consistent data. It works well for data sets such as bank account and credit card statements.

While technology suggests matches for many transactions, your teams still review them, and look out for exceptions and anything that might raise a red flag.

However, agentic AI, such as Sage Copilot, can even handle this element.

It’s worth adding, though, that light-touch reconciliations require high-quality, accurately collated data—via technology that can easily and correctly identify these anomalies. Human review remains essential.

The decades-old mantra of technology has always been “garbage in, garbage out”, and so it’s essential that your clients record and submit data correctly.

Direct bank feeds from clients can help here, by importing transactions as timely digital records, as can data capture tools like AutoEntry, which can read receipts or bills and pass the data to you for processing. These tools import, suggest, or flag information. They don’t replace reconciliation, checks for missing information, or a review of tax categories.

You can use technology like this to help automate processes and reduce the chance of manual data entry errors that can occur when human beings have to copy from one statement or spreadsheet to another.

You can then set up this software to suggest categories for the various items that pop up on a bank feed, for your team to check, for your HMRC submissions and interactions.

For instance, you’ll need to strip out your clients’ non-taxable income and any personal expenditure they might have. You should also adjust any items of income that are net of fees, commissions, or charges before doing clients’ tax returns to ensure that you’re declaring gross income but then netting off these expenses.

What is a digital record-keeping stack, and why do you need one?

A digital record-keeping stack is a set of integrated tools that captures client income and expenditure digitally and carries it through to quarterly updates and the final tax return, with no rekeying.

The fundamentals are that you need to build an end-to-end digital record keeping stack. 

If you’ve already got one in place, you’ll need to ensure not only that it’s fit for purpose in the age of MTD, but that it’s allowing your practice to run at optimal efficiency. There simply isn’t likely to be any spare human capacity.

This end-to-end digital outlook is important. It’s one step beyond traditional, stand-alone technologies, and the end of processes to which paperwork is fundamental.

Instead, you’ll need to ensure that you’ve got technologies in place that are integrated with each other. This means that they can work together as a single system to manage and process your digital records and those of your clients efficiently and in ways that comply with regulations and cybersecurity protocols. Digital linking is as important as it ever was!

As a result, client income and expenditure can be recorded fully digitally, from the start to the finish. 

Your technology stack should ensure that these records of income and outgoings are automatically ingested into quarterly updates before going through to the final year end declaration.

You’ll need to ensure that this happens automatically and seamlessly. Manually typing in figures and details and even copying and pasting them from one source or spreadsheet to another is not only inefficient—it also breaks the digital linking rule: enter once, and use digital links after. That means no copy and paste, and no rekeying, of the core tax records.

Instead, you should be deploying software that is fully integrated and offers an end-to-end solution for you and your clients so that there are no messy transfers or transitions between your systems and those of your clients.

For more on rebuilding your practice around MTD, read MTD for Income Tax is an operational reset—and the best reason to rebuild your firm’s foundations.

Should clients use bridging software for MTD?

Bridging software lets clients who keep suitable spreadsheets meet MTD rules, and it can remain a compliant option for the long term. Whether a client would benefit from moving to bookkeeping software depends on how they work.

You might find that some clients on spreadsheets are struggling with the transition, in which case you could consider using bridging software.

This provides a link between old-style record-keeping, such as spreadsheets, on one side and HMRC’s systems on the other.

Bridging software isn’t only a temporary fix: suitable spreadsheets used with compatible bridging software can remain compliant. That said, HMRC notes the trade-off:

“Keep in mind, spreadsheets won’t have the same timesaving, user-friendly features as many all-in-one bookkeeping apps.”

If clients use it, make sure their spreadsheets are set up to keep the required digital records and that data moves through digital links. For some clients, moving to bookkeeping software later may save time, but it isn’t a requirement.

As you implement the digitisation process, you might find that other clients also have their own, specific requirements.

Sole traders and smaller landlords, for instance, will probably find mobile-first bookkeeping most useful. This is entirely feasible. The days of always requiring a desktop PC are gone.

Similarly, you should already be encouraging other clients whose work means that they’re out and about to use apps on their smartphones. This can be useful for making and taking payments that feed directly into the system in real time and, as mentioned earlier, for taking photos of receipts whose amounts, details and dates can be automatically read by the technology and fed into the system.

How does client management software help with MTD?

Client management software automates deadline reminders, client requests, approvals, and document sharing, so more frequent MTD contact doesn’t mean more admin.

As you move to a digital-first way of working, it’s also a good idea to implement client management software.

This can manage tasks and workflows such as notifications for deadlines for submissions as well as automatically recording billable hours.

Increasingly, specialist agentic AI can help with critical tasks. Sage’s MTD for IT Agent can help with many of them, while your team reviews and approves the results.

It’s designed to help with complex, interconnected tasks: for example, it can organise data and highlight anomalies for your team to review. Features include drafting quarterly submission reports and preparing document requests to clients. The time saved varies by practice and client.

Read more in How agentic AI is changing accounting compliance.

Other parts of client management software provide insights into staff workloads and performance as well as revealing the profitability of particular clients. You’ll be able to identify more quickly and accurately whether you’re charging enough—or even overcharging—for each account.

As communication with clients becomes more frequent and data is shared more often, client management systems can take on much of this. Routine emails, requests for permissions and approvals plus notifications can be managed automatically.

Similarly, client management systems can enable you to share documents and data with clients as well as managing e-signatures more quickly and easily. You can also use them to set up client interaction portals so that your clients know how to submit data and share documents as well as signing them digitally.

What do your teams need to know about MTD for Income Tax?

Your teams need to move from inputting data to reviewing it: know your cloud bookkeeping software, spot exceptions, and guide clients through the new deadlines.

As well as implementing these new technologies, you should be training staff and helping them to develop a new mindset.

They need to become familiar now with cloud bookkeeping software and to be ready to review and understand data rather than simply inputting it manually and using it to carry out calculations. They should be ready to identify exceptions to this data and their significance as well as understanding more generally how they should interact with MTD for Income Tax technology.

Your teams need to be ready to answer clients’ questions and to guide them on how to comply with the new deadlines, requirements and ways of working. They should be showing clients how to use the new technologies and checking on their progress as they provide ongoing support.

This is a major change to the way that accountants work and interact with their clients. However, you can lead them through the process and cement your role as business advisers as well as ensuring that you’re compliant with HMRC’s new Making Tax Digital requirements. Better still, reducing repetitive, manual processes will free up your teams to carry out more interesting, fulfilling tasks and to add more value.

Switching to MTD for Income Tax: FAQs

			

			

	

What changes when a client moves from Self Assessment to MTD for Income Tax?

	

			

Clients moving to MTD for Income Tax must keep digital records in MTD-compatible software and send four quarterly updates a year, plus an annual Self Assessment return by 31 January, filed through compatible software.

	

	

Will practices still need to handle Self Assessment?

	

			

Yes. Clients below the MTD threshold stay on Self Assessment, and the threshold falls in stages to £20,000 by April 2028, so most practices will run both systems side by side for several years.

	

	

Can clients keep using spreadsheets for MTD for Income Tax?

	

			

Yes. Clients can use suitable spreadsheets with compatible bridging software that links the spreadsheet to HMRC digitally, and this can remain compliant. HMRC notes that spreadsheets won’t have the same timesaving features as many bookkeeping apps.

	

	

What technology does a practice need for MTD?

	

			

A practice needs an integrated, end-to-end digital record-keeping stack: bookkeeping software, bank feeds, data capture tools such as AutoEntry, and client management software, with digital links between them.

	

	

How should practices prepare their teams for MTD?

	

			

Practices should train staff on cloud bookkeeping software, and help them shift from inputting data to reviewing it, spotting exceptions, and guiding clients through the quarterly cycle.

Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax is the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) requirement for sole traders and landlords within scope to keep digital records, send quarterly updates to HMRC, and file their annual Self Assessment tax return, all using MTD-compatible software. It started on 6 April 2026 for those with qualifying income above £50,000.

Key takeaways

MTD for Income Tax applies in phases: sole traders and landlords with qualifying gross income above £50,000 from April 2026, above £30,000 from April 2027, and above £20,000 from April 2028.

Only self-employment and property income counts towards the threshold—other income, such as savings interest, is ignored.

Clients within scope must keep digital records, send quarterly updates, and file their annual Self Assessment tax return by 31 January, all using MTD-compatible software.

Quarterly updates are cumulative (year to date) and are due by 7 August, 7 November, 7 February, and 7 May, and no tax is paid when an update is sent.

As the client’s main agent, you can submit the annual return once your client has reviewed it and confirmed in writing that it’s correct and complete. Quarterly updates can be submitted by you, a supporting agent such as their bookkeeper, or the client.

There can be few accountants and bookkeepers who haven’t heard of MTD for Income Tax. With the first introduction date of April 2026 now passed, you might still have work to do to get your practice ready.

This article can help. Read on to learn how you can get to grips with MTD for Income Tax across everything you do, regardless of the size of your practice or the nature of your clients.

Are you a sole trader or landlord looking for MTD for Income Tax guidance? Get our dedicated guide, written by experts

Here’s what this article discusses:

What is Making Tax Digital for Income Tax?

MTD for Income Tax is a new way for sole traders and landlords to record and report their income to HMRC. The government has said MTD for Income Tax is being mandated in at least three phases.

It affects sole traders and landlords (or individuals who are both) that have gross income above £50,000 from April 2026, above £30,000 from April 2027, and above £20,000 from April 2028.

As happened with MTD for VAT, clients will turn to accountants for advice and guidance. 

More than this, the government is again likely relying at least partially on accountants to educate their clients about the requirements and ongoing process adaptations.

It’s vital to realise how Making Tax Digital for Income Tax provides opportunities:

Clients can modernise their accounting processes, to get the benefits of massively reduced admin and a closer, more active relationship with their accountant. Considering AI productivity assistants are now within accounting software, the improvements could be revolutionary—and not as technically onerous compared to the old days.

Accountants have an opportunity to grow their services via increased client touchpoints through quarterly updates and the digital tax return—not to mention initial guidance on signing up, adjusting admin processes, and helping with software choices. Better and accurate visibility into client data can inspire a vast range of services.

If your practice has income tax clients that fall under the scope of MTD for Income Tax, you need to start putting plans into practice today, if you haven’t already. The scale of clients impacted, which is significantly higher than for VAT a few years ago, means the quantity of work cannot be underestimated.

When does MTD for Income Tax start for my client’s business?

Your client’s MTD for Income Tax start date depends on their qualifying gross income from self-employment and property:

MTD for Income Tax start date

Qualifying gross income

Based on income in tax year

6 April 2026

Above £50,000

2024/25

6 April 2027

Above £30,000

2025/26

6 April 2028

Above £20,000

2026/27

MTD for Income Tax applies from 6 April of the relevant tax year: 6 April 2026 if qualifying income from self-employment and property on the 2024/25 return was above £50,000, 6 April 2027 if it was above £30,000 on the 2025/26 return, and 6 April 2028 if it was above £20,000 on the 2026/27 return. Your client must keep digital records from that 6 April, and their quarterly update periods follow the tax year (or calendar quarters, if they choose), whatever their accounting date.

HMRC will inform clients in writing if they need to use MTD for Income Tax.

From September 2026, HMRC is also signing up sole traders and landlords who are required to use MTD for Income Tax but haven’t registered. Find out more in HMRC-led sign-up for MTD for Income Tax: What accountants need to know.

For accounting periods before their MTD start date, those within scope will continue to use the Self Assessment system for the business.

For example, a client who started MTD for Income Tax on 6 April 2026 still files their 2025/26 Self Assessment return in the usual way by 31 January 2027 (or by 30 December 2026 if they want HMRC to collect tax through their PAYE tax code, where eligible). From 2026/27 onwards, their annual Self Assessment return is filed through compatible software.

Individuals outside the scope of MTD for Income Tax may still need to file a Self Assessment return in the usual way. Being below the MTD threshold, being a company director, or receiving pension income doesn’t on its own mean someone must file, so check HMRC’s Self Assessment filing criteria for each client.

Which clients will be affected by MTD for Income Tax and how?

To fall under the MTD for Income Tax scope, all of the £50,000/£30,000/£20,000+ income will have to come from either sole trade businesses, or property rents, or a combination of both. No other income matters for this calculation. 

For example:

For example, should one of your clients have just £49,000 from property rental to declare for income tax, and £2,000 from savings interest income, that won’t require them to sign up for MTD for Income Tax. All of this is before allowable expenses, of course.

But if they had £45,000 from sole trade income and £10,000 from property rental income, then their gross income will be £55,000—pushing them above the threshold of the April 2026 rollout, for example. HMRC bases their decision for this based on the gross income for the 2024/25 tax year, as shown on the Self Assessment tax return.

Care needs to be taken, however, because for some clients, 2024/25 may have had an unusually long basis period because of basis period reform (BPR) measures. Therefore, their earnings might be artificially high. If you believe this is the case for your client, and that their income is typically below the threshold, contact HMRC to discuss the issue.

Those new to a sole trader or property rental will use the Self Assessment system, and never go straight to using MTD for Income Tax, even if it’s clear their income will rise above £50,000 (or £30,000/£20,000 as of 2027/2028). 

Effectively, this means these clients will always complete two years of Self Assessment prior to moving to MTD for Income Tax, unless they opt to voluntarily do sign-up. This can be done even if their earnings are below the threshold. If this option is chosen, the client will complete a single year’s Self Assessment before moving to MTD for Income Tax at the start of the subsequent tax year.

What are MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates and the digital tax return?

Quarterly updates are cumulative summaries of income and expenses sent to HMRC during the year, and the annual tax return is the Self Assessment return, which clients in MTD file through compatible software.

MTD for Income Tax doesn’t abolish Self Assessment. Clients signed up to MTD still file one annual Self Assessment tax return for each tax year, but they submit it through compatible software rather than HMRC’s online service or a paper SA100.

In addition, they send quarterly updates using compatible software, as follows, and file the annual return by 31 January.

Here are the MTD for Income Tax requirements in brief:

Digital records for MTD for Income Tax

A digital record is a line item of income or expense, which is to say, each transaction. The minimum data that needs to be recorded is as follows:

Amount.

Date.

The tax category, as defined by HMRC, such as turnover, cost of goods bought for resale, or wages, salaries and other staff costs. Car, van and travel expenses are also categorised. 

Obviously, MTD-compatible accounting software will make it easy to record these details via automation.

None of this is outside the scope of data already recorded for Self Assessment, of course. The difference is simply that it must be recorded ASAP, and certainly prior to any quarterly update submission. 

Quarterly updates for MTD for Income Tax

Quarterly update deadlines are the same every year:

Quarterly update

Period ending

Latest submission date

First update

5 July

7 August

5 October

7 November

Third update

5 January

7 February
