7 May

These are generated in MTD-compatible software by you or the client. You or their bookkeeper can submit them on behalf of the client.

Each update gives cumulative year-to-date totals for each income and expense category, from the start of the tax year to the end of the latest period. HMRC does not require individual income or expenditure records at this point, or for the tax return.

The deadlines in the table apply even if the client uses the fiscal year (1 April to 31 March) for their basis period.

An update doesn’t include any obligation or statement that the data is complete and accurate, and no tax is paid at that point.

If something in an earlier period was wrong, correct it in the digital records. The correction then flows through in the next cumulative update (or in the annual return, after the final update).

HMRC returns a calculation of the estimated tax liability based on the information sent. This should be discussed with clients, with potential inaccuracies notified (pending later adjustments).

For a step-by-step process, read MTD quarterly updates: A practice guide for accountants and bookkeepers. To understand what happens if an update is late, see Making Tax Digital for Income Tax penalties: HMRC’s new systems explained and the MTD for Income Tax penalty delay (soft landing period) explained.

Digital tax return for MTD for Income Tax

Very similar to Self Assessment, the tax return is to be completed and submitted via MTD-compatible software at the end of the tax period or any point after this date and up to the following 31 January.

A separate Business Source Adjustable Summary (BSAS) can be requested from HMRC, via the MTD-compatible software, for each business and property income. This is the foundation used by accountants to make adjustments for each income source, such as capital allowances, private use adjustments, corrections, and disallowable expenses. Accountants should not simply use the fourth quarterly update as the numbers for the tax return. BSAS totals are not a substitute for completing the digital tax return and accountants must make adjustments as required.

Remember that the MTD rules mean any adjustments/corrections must be undertaken in MTD-compatible software and legally-compliant digital links must be used between software and systems if data is transferred (e.g. from a spreadsheet to accounting software—it is not legally possible to cut/copy and paste data). 

The submission is a declaration that the information is complete and correct. The client must review and sign. As with Self Assessment, you are unable to do this for them.

Once submitted, HMRC returns a tax calculation.

The digital tax return effectively replaces the SA100 tax return. Additionally:

31 January continues to be the deadline for filing.

Any income tax liability must also be paid by 31 January (payments on account will continue).

HMRC will not provide any submission interface to allow filing without the need for software. In other words, MTD-compatible software must be used all the way through. If more than one piece of software or system is used, it must be digitally linked in a legally-compliant way.

If any information that needs to be included in the final declaration isn’t supported via software submission, then the client will also need to complete a Self Assessment tax return.

However, if data cannot be submitted digitally for whatever reason, then a SA100 may still be required. 

Supplementary forms for income tax like SA102, SA105 and so forth, are no longer required because of the use of quarterly updates to provide the data or the fact the software is connected to HMRC, so can automatically pull in detais like employment income. 

What information will clients submit for MTD for Income Tax?

Clients submit income, expenses, allowances, and adjustments for each self-employment and property business, plus other income, such as dividends and savings interest, in the tax return.

The following lists aren’t exhaustive, so check HMRC’s guidance for the full requirements.

The following are non-exhaustive lists and subject to change and confirmation by HMRC.

For a self-employment business, the data required includes:

Business income (e.g. turnover)

Business expenses (total and disallowable by type of expense, such as travel costs)

Tax allowances for vehicles and equipment (e.g. capital allowances)

Adjustments (e.g. basis adjustment)

Balancing charges

Goods and services for client’s own use.

For a property business, the data required includes:

UK and foreign property business income

UK and foreign property business expenses (e.g. premises running costs)

Allowances for property (e.g. annual investment allowance)

Adjustments on property letting (e.g. loss brought forward)

Balancing charges.

For the tax return, the individual must also include the following, among other things:

Total UK dividend income for a tax year

Taxed UK savings interest

Untaxed UK savings interest

Other income sources

Any claims or elections.

Can clients opt out of MTD for Income Tax?

As with MTD for VAT, it won’t be possible for most clients to opt out of MTD for Income Tax if they fall within its scope.

However, if they joined voluntarily in the public beta, they can opt out.

And that’s also the case if they’re in specific categories that are automatically exempt, including:

Trustees

Personal representatives

Foster carers

Those without a National Insurance number in the January before the start of the tax year.

Non-resident companies.

Those who fall under the digital exclusion rules as defined by MTD for VAT will automatically be exempted from MTD for Income Tax (although there will be no harm in checking this!).

This includes people whose disabilities mean they can’t use software, for example, for people whose remote location means internet access is impossible.

Additionally, your clients will be exempt from Making Tax Digital if their qualifying income falls below the threshold for three consecutive tax years (bearing in mind this threshold will fall each year after 2026, until reaching £20,000 for 2028/29.

Clients will require MTD-compatible software of some kind. Understandably, they may look for free solutions. Sage Sole Trader is a great example, and can help clients with simple tax affairs manage their finances with software that makes bookkeeping, transaction tracking, and both MTD for Income Tax and Self Assessment easy.

However, as an accounting professional, you will require them to have more sophisticated software if you intend to collaborate with them for quarterly updates and the tax return. There are a variety of Sage Accounting plans to meet both yours and your client needs, and will grow in features as they grow, too. Examples include VAT accounting and payroll. You can access more information on our MTD for accountants hub page.

A Sage for Accountants plan offers the chance to upsell Sage Accounting directly to clients, and comes with a host of free software for accountants, such as Final Accounts and Tax, Client Management, plus free AutoEntry, GoProposal and Futrli credits each month.

Most of the big-name cloud accounting software has already been updated for MTD for Income Tax, although this might not necessarily be true for desktop accounting software. You or your clients may need to consult the software vendor to ensure updates and patches are installed.

Older software packages that are no longer supported may not be updated, so might require the client migrate their accounting to a different package.

It will be possible to use spreadsheets for MTD for Income Tax accounting through the use of either bridging software, or special spreadsheets/worksheets that facilitate digital linking with cloud services.

Remember that the digital linking rules say that copying and pasting of MTD accounting records is not allowed, and all transfer of MTD for Income Tax data must be both digital and automated.

Because of this and other issues, using a spreadsheet is unlikely to be the most user-friendly solution.

Additionally, MTD-compatible software must be able to:

Create and store digital records

Send quarterly updates

Submit the final declaration

Receive information from HMRC.

What is digital linking for MTD for Income Tax?

Digital linking means relevant tax data must follow a fully digital path once it has entered the system. You may recall the digital linking rules from the implementation of MTD for VAT.

In summary, it aims to legally enforce a fully digital path for relevant tax data once it has entered the system. 

For example, once an expense record is entered into accounting software, that value cannot then be copied into a spreadsheet for further processing, before being pasted back. The expense record must be transferred digitally by the software, via the cloud, for example. 

There’s less of a focus on digital linking in MTD for Income Tax because there are likely to be fewer interconnected applications or systems compared to VAT. But it still applies if spreadsheets are in use, as a key example, and could impact retail clients who use electronic point of sale (EPOS) systems with accounting software, or who use online auction software. 

In such a case, the two (or more) systems must be digitally linked in a legally compliant way, typically by sharing data in the cloud (e.g. the EPOS system will be available as an add-in extension for the accounting software, via the accounting software’s App Store).

Furthermore, if you work with clients then you’ll need to ensure data transfer happens digitally (although emailing and transferring files via a USB memory stick are acceptable). 

Do clients signed up for MTD for VAT need to sign up for MTD for Income Tax?

Not automatically. Clients signed up for MTD for VAT only need to sign up for MTD for Income Tax if they meet its own criteria. The two Making Tax Digital schemes for VAT and Income Tax operate independently, with their own sign up criteria.

It isn’t the case that MTD for Income Tax applies only to those already using MTD for VAT—although many businesses already using MTD for VAT will find themselves having to sign up for MTD for Income Tax too.

What are the MTD for Income Tax easements for clients?

HMRC has provided easements for joint property owners, businesses using three-line accounts, and retail businesses recording daily takings. Following feedback, HMRC has provided a handful of easements to assist certain kinds of businesses:

Joint property ownership

A joint owner of a property only needs to submit their own share of income and expenses (e.g. one record for each), and not the full figures for the property. 

They will need to provide records for total rent, other income from the property, premiums for the grant of a lease, and reverse premiums and inducements. For expenses, records should include property repairs and maintenance, residential finance costs, professional fees, and more (for more details, see sections 2.1 and 2.2 of HMRC’s MTD for Income Tax Update Notice).

Each joint owner will need to separately and independently follow the MTD for Income Tax rules, however, such as using MTD-compatible software. Furthermore, legally-compliant digital linking is required between applications and systems. Landlords who use spreadsheets to track depreciation of assets cannot copy and paste data into their accounting software, for example. In situations like this, use of professional MTD-compatible property management software is advisable. 

Three-line accounts

Already possible for Self Assessment, this easement can also be used for MTD for Income Tax. 

Clients with an annual turnover below the VAT registration threshold (currently £90,000) may opt to submit total income and expenses rather than breaking these figures down by tax category.

However, given the requirement to keep digital records of income and expenditure in any event, and the use of MTD-compatible software that will automatically produce detailed quarterly updates and a tax return based on those records, it’s unclear how useful this easement will be.

Retail sales

Clients may choose to record the daily gross takings for all retail sales as a single digital record. This must include all payments from cash paying customers, plus credit sales, gift card redemptions, sales competed via third-party booking platforms, and so on. For more details, see section 3 of HMRC’s MTD for Income Tax Digital Record Keeping Notice.

What does MTD for Income Tax mean for accountants?

MTD for Income Tax means more frequent client contact, a bigger role in software choices, and new opportunities for advisory work. It’s hard to overstate the changes it will bring for you.

Here are two things to be aware of:

1. Your clients will have to use software

Your clients will be required to use compatible software to record their business and property income and expenditure and send five updates/reports every year to HMRC.

There’s likely to be automation for each of these steps, minimising the administrative impact. But your clients still need to be aware of the requirements expected of them.

This will require a substantial change in attitude from your clients in how they approach their accounting.

It’s certainly the case that the “shoebox” client who dumps receipts on their accountant’s desk in January each year will have to change their ways.

It’s your role to communicate this need for change, and to encourage it to happen.

In return, you’ re given significant privilege to guide your clients towards the best solution for their needs—and to bring positive changes to their clients’ businesses.

This presents additional opportunities.

Not partnering with a software vendor to sell solutions to your clients, for example, is to discard a potentially large income source.

Needless to say, an MTD for Income Tax-compatible cloud accounting solution that ties into your own systems is best for both you and your client.

You can offer training in the software, perhaps as part of the sales package, or as a separate service offering.

At the very least, every UK accountant will need to be proficient in the MTD-compatible software their clients use, because accountants will be facing client enquiries about this on a very regular basis.

2. You have the opportunity to offer additional advisory services

Although MTD for Income Tax should mean clients are more aware of their accounting, it doesn’t mean your fundamental role will change.

You’ll still be required to help your clients be compliant, and to support them with fundamentals such as making deductions and calculating a final income tax bill.

While it’s possible some small business owners may have an epiphany moment when they get to grips with accounting software and realise the power it delivers, the fundamental fact that many people hate dealing with figures and the ensuing admin burden isn’t going to change.

You have nothing to fear from technology and, in fact, lots to gain.

But this is only scratching the surface of the potential that MTD for Income Tax will deliver.

You’ll go from having a single point of contact each year to potentially having at least five situations where your clients may need help with their accounting when they make those quarterly reports and the final declaration.

These situations can be used to forge stronger relationships where you’re not viewed as just a number cruncher but more of a business partner.

Using cloud software that ties in with your clients’ accounting gives you the ability to monitor for problems or opportunities, and to provide advice based on this.

For ideas on how to package and price this ongoing work, read Pricing for MTD: How to charge more, and prove it’s worth it.

Final thoughts on MTD for Income Tax

If your practice dealt with the implementation of MTD for VAT ahead of it being mandated in April 2019, you’ll be well aware that starting early with preparations will put you and your clients in good stead.

If it didn’t, the best advice is to start now.

Look at your processes, start talking to your clients, and take the steps now to not only meet the requirements for MTD for Income Tax but to use it as an opportunity to help your practice and your clients really flourish.

MTD for Income Tax for accountants: FAQs

			

			

	

Who has to use MTD for Income Tax?

	

			

Sole traders and landlords with qualifying gross income above £50,000 from April 2026, above £30,000 from April 2027, and above £20,000 from April 2028. Only income from self-employment and property counts towards the threshold.

	

	

When are MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates due?

	

			

Quarterly updates give cumulative year-to-date figures and must be sent by 7 August, 7 November, 7 February, and 7 May, covering the quarters ending 5 July, 5 October, 5 January, and 5 April. No tax is paid when an update is sent.

	

	

Do clients still need to file a Self Assessment tax return?

	

			

Yes. MTD for Income Tax doesn’t abolish Self Assessment. Clients starting in April 2026 file their 2025/26 return in the usual way by 31 January 2027. From 2026/27, they still file one annual Self Assessment return, but through compatible software.

	

	

Can an accountant submit the digital tax return for a client?

	

			

Yes, if you’re the client’s main agent. You must check the calculation, share the return with your client for review, and get their written confirmation that it’s correct and complete before you submit it through compatible software. Supporting agents, such as a bookkeeper, can submit quarterly updates but not the annual return.

	

	

Can clients use spreadsheets for MTD for Income Tax?

	

			

Yes, clients can use spreadsheets, but only with bridging software or spreadsheets that facilitate digital linking with cloud services. Copying and pasting MTD accounting records isn’t allowed, but a spreadsheet used with compatible bridging software is a valid option.

fullText:
Key takeaways

MTD for Income Tax is live. It became law for sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000 on 6 April 2026.

It’s had a difficult history since its inception in 2015, with several postponements and rescoping of who/what is included. But that’s all history now. 

The £30,000 threshold applies from 6 April 2027. The £20,000 threshold applies from 6 April 2028.

No penalty points for late quarterly updates in 2026/27. From 2027/28, each missed deadline earns a point, with a £200 penalty at four.

It’s a fair question. Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax was first pencilled in for 2018, then 2023, then 2024, before landing on April 2026.

The good news? That pattern is now broken and MTD is steaming ahead. Any further cancellations or postponements are very unlikely. 

The first wave is in, covering incomes over £50,000 and, at the time of publication, the first quarterly updates have been filed.

What’s more, HMRC is actively signing up people who haven’t done so themselves. 

The question isn’t “will it happen” any more. It’s “which date applies to me, and am I ready for it?”.

Let’s take a closer look, as follows:

Is MTD delayed in 2026/2027/2028? The short answer is…

No. 

GOV.UK confirms that if your qualifying income was over £50,000 in 2024/25, you should already be using MTD for Income Tax, and that if you haven’t signed up you still can.

HMRC and the UK government’s position is that MTD is now a legal requirement and that anyone in scope should check they’re signed up, their software is compatible, and their update is in before the deadline.

One thing did soften, and it’s probably feeding any rumour you may have heard: HMRC won’t apply penalty points for late quarterly updates in the 2026/27 tax year. 

That’s a soft landing on lateness, not a pause. The obligation to keep digital records and send updates stands.

The official and confirmed MTD deadlines from 2026 and 2027 onwards

HMRC publishes the full timeline on its Making Tax Digital campaign site and in the quarterly updates guidance on GOV.UK. 

For anyone already in the first wave, the next dates at the time of publication are as follows. 

Watch out for some gotchas, such as deadlines occurring over the weekend:

7 November 2026: 2nd quarterly update (covering 6 April to 5 October). Falls on a Saturday.

31 January 2027: Your 2025/26 Self Assessment return, filed the usual way.

7 February 2027: 3rd quarterly update. Falls on a Sunday.

6 April 2027: The £30,000 wave kicks off, and those included should start keeping digital records.

7 May 2027: 4th quarterly update. Falls on a Friday.

7 August 2027: First quarterly update of 2027/28, for both those included in the £50,000 wave and those included in the £30,000 wave.

31 January 2028: The first MTD tax return for 2026/27, with any required tax payment due the same day. This covers all your sources of income, unlike quarterly updates, which are limited to income and expenditure. 

A detail worth diarising: Three of the next four quarterly deadlines fall on a weekend, and January/February 2027 stacks a Self Assessment return and then an MTD quarterly update a week apart. 

If you rely on an accountant, that’s their busiest fortnight of the year, so make sure you get everything over to them well ahead of time.

Who’s affected, and when

GOV.UK’s rule is simple to state. You need MTD for Income Tax if you’re a sole trader or landlord registered for Self Assessment and your qualifying income is over the threshold for that tax year:

Over £50,000 in 2024/25: You should’ve started on 6 April 2026.

Over £30,000 in 2025/26: You start on 6 April 2027.

Over £20,000 in 2026/27: You start on 6 April 2028.

Partnerships will follow at a date HMRC hasn’t yet set. You can check your own position with HMRC’s online tool.

Will Making Tax Digital spread to other taxes?

MTD already covers VAT, and is in the process of rolling out to apply to Income Tax: sole traders and landlords earning over £50,000 join from April 2026, over £30,000 from April 2027 and over £20,000 from April 2028. 

Beyond that, HMRC has pulled back. Its July 2025 Transformation Roadmap stated: “HMRC does not intend to introduce MTD for Corporation Tax“. 

So, limited companies keep filing annual returns as now. 

HMRC is still exploring digitalisation for sole traders below £20,000, and aims to be “digital-first” by 2030 through pre-populated returns, AI tools, and possible e-invoicing.

6 lesser-known MTD details that catch people out

1. It’s turnover, not profit

The single most common question in the first quarter was still “does this apply to me?”, usually confusing profit with turnover and unsure which income sources count. 

Qualifying income is gross income from self-employment and property, combined. A side business plus a rental flat can tip you over together even if neither does alone.

2. No letter doesn’t mean no obligation

HMRC writes to people it believes are in scope, but HMRC is explicit that if you don’t receive a letter it’s still your responsibility to check and sign up, if required.

3. The £20,000 wave is a different animal

The smallest cohort will often have simpler accounts but a harder journey: lower software adoption, more “once a year in a shoebox” habits, more landlords with mixed income, and far more people with no accountant acting as translator. 

If you earn around £20,000 from a trade or a rental, the honest truth is that accounting has probably never been something you took seriously. 

From April 2028, you’ll need to. Start now, and make life easier for yourself.

4. Preparing and filing are different moments

Many people signed up and connected their software weeks early, then waited until the final days to send the update. The deadline created its own peak. 

Build a habit of sending the update as soon as the quarter closes.

5. Updates are cumulative, so mistakes should self-correct

Each update covers from 6 April to the end of the period. 

This means you can fix any data that was wrong, and the correction flows into the next update automatically. You’ve no need to specifically call anything out as a mistake.

6. Nil updates still count

If you had no income or expenses in a period, you still have to send the update.

Final thoughts

MTD for Income Tax isn’t delayed, and it’s unlikely it will be from this point onwards.

The people who had the smoothest first quarter weren’t lucky. They’d got software in place early, kept bookkeeping ticking over weekly, and set internal deadlines ahead of the statutory ones.

The 2026/27 year is the cheapest it will ever be to learn the rhythm, because lateness won’t cost penalty points. From 2027/28, it will.

Takeaway: check your 2025/26 turnover now. If it’s over £30,000, your start date is 6 April 2027 and your first deadline is 7 August 2027. If it’s over £20,000, you’ve got until April 2028, but the habits take longer to build than the software does.

MTD delays and postponement FAQs

			

			

	

Has MTD for Income Tax been delayed again in 2026?

	

			

No. It went live on 6 April 2026 for qualifying income over £50,000 and the first quarterly update deadline has already passed.

	

	

Will the £30,000 threshold be delayed?

	

			

GOV.UK currently states 6 April 2027 for qualifying income over £30,000 in 2025/26, and no change has been announced.

	

	

Does MTD change when I pay tax?

	

			

No. Your tax return and payment are still due by 31 January after the tax year ends; for 2026/27 that’s 31 January 2028. Ditto for any payments on account required by HMRC, which are also due on 31 July.

	

	

Will MTD apply to Corporation Tax?

	

			

No. HMRC originally planned for this to be the case, but has since permanently cancelled that project. 

Although Corporation Tax accounting and filing might be digitalised in other ways moving forward, at the moment it’s still built around keeping compliant accounting records and submitting a Corporation Tax return—just as it has been for decades.

		

	

	

Will MTD apply to taxes like Inheritance Tax or Capital Gains?

	

			

No. Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax applies to qualifying income from self-employment and property. HMRC confirms that other sources of income, such as employment, pensions and dividends, do not count towards the qualifying-income thresholds, although they may still need to be included in the taxpayer’s overall digital tax return on 31 January.

Capital Gains Tax (CGT) is reported through separate HMRC digital services or Self Assessment, rather than through MTD’s quarterly updates. UK residential property gains must generally be reported, and any CGT due paid, within 60 days of completion. Other taxable gains can be reported through HMRC’s real-time CGT service by 31 December in the tax year following the disposal, with payment due by 31 January, or through Self Assessment. Where a taxpayer uses MTD for Income Tax, other taxable income and gains must still be included in the annual digital tax return, normally by 31 January.

Inheritance Tax is being digitalised separately. HMRC’s Transformation Roadmap, updated in 2026, confirms plans to replace the existing paper-based process with an end-to-end digital service from the 2027/28 tax year.

		

	

	

Are any MTD quarterly updates delayed, postponed, or cancelled? 

	

			

The simple yet complete answer is no! See the body of this article for a list of deadlines. 

	

	

Is the MTD for Income Tax digital tax return delayed, postponed, or cancelled?

	

			

No. You should submit this via your MTD-ready software by 31 January. Bear in mind that, although HMRC is not enforcing penalties if you miss an MTD quarterly deadline in the first year of MTD for Income Tax (2026/27), this does not extend to the tax return deadline—they are likely to impose penalties if you miss it!

fullText:
The Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax soft landing period is first-year penalty relief for sole traders and landlords mandated from April 2026. Late submission of the first four quarterly updates doesn’t attract penalty points, and late payment penalties don’t arise for up to 30 days. You still need to keep digital records, submit quarterly updates, and file your 2026/27 tax return by 31 January 2028.

Key takeaways

No penalty points for late quarterly updates in your first year: if you were mandated from April 2026, late submission of the first four quarterly updates (due 7 August 2026, 7 November 2026, 7 February 2027, and 7 May 2027) doesn’t attract penalty points.

The tax return isn’t covered: penalties apply if your 2026/27 tax return, due by 31 January 2028, is late.

Late payment penalties don’t arise for up to 30 days in your first year, although interest on unpaid tax may still run.

Your obligations don’t change: HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) still expects digital records from your MTD start date, and quarterly updates.

From 2027/28, penalty points apply: quarterly filers get a £200 penalty at four points, and another £200 for every late submission after that.

For many sole traders and landlords, the April 2026 start date of MTD for Income Tax might have come as a surprise, leaving them playing catch-up.

However, announcements at the 2025 Autumn Budget introduced a welcome “soft landing” period with penalty relief, designed to smooth the transition to MTD—and in particular, digital record-keeping and quarterly submissions.

Care needs to be taken, though. This definitely isn’t a get-out-of-jail-free card.

This article breaks down these crucial HMRC MTD for Income Tax updates, explaining how to take advantage of the MTD for Income Tax soft landing period. It also looks at how the new penalty points system works.

Here’s what this article discusses:

The soft landing period is penalty relief for your first year of MTD for Income Tax: late quarterly updates don’t attract penalty points, and late payment penalties don’t arise for up to 30 days.

The updates that arrived with the 2025 Autumn Budget bring welcome clarity and flexibility, designed to make your initial steps with MTD for Income Tax significantly more manageable.

1. First-year penalty relief for quarterly updates

HMRC has confirmed that, for taxpayers mandated for MTD for Income Tax from April 2026, late submission of the first four quarterly updates does not attract penalty points, provided other conditions are met.

This penalty relief does not apply to your end-of-year MTD tax return for 2026/27, which is due by 31 January 2028. Penalties apply for late submission of this final, annual declaration.

To be clear, once you’ve started MTD for Income Tax, from year two onwards penalties apply for late submission of quarterly updates due from 7 August 2027 onwards, as shown in the table above.

Furthermore, the government has not confirmed if the soft landing period will apply to those starting MTD for Income Tax in April 2027 (for the £30,000 gross qualifying income threshold), or April 2028 (for the £20,000 gross qualifying income threshold). More may be confirmed as those dates approach, but nothing is certain.

What this means for those starting MTD for Income Tax in April 2026: This provision offers a crucial grace period.

It’s your opportunity to learn the ropes of MTD-compatible software, refine your digital record-keeping processes, and understand the quarterly submission routine without the immediate pressure of penalty points.

Just remember that HMRC still expects you to maintain digital records from your MTD start date, and submit quarterly updates.

So, think of it as an opportunity to iron out any creases in your new system.

2. Extended grace period for late payments

During your first year in the new penalty system, HMRC will, in the first year, allow up to 30 days before late payment penalties arise under the new regime, although interest on unpaid tax may still run.

What this means: This enhanced grace period provides invaluable flexibility for your cash flow management. As you adapt to potentially new ways of monitoring your tax liability, it allows you a little more time to ensure funds are available without incurring immediate penalties.

3. Deferrals and exemptions for specific groups

Recognising unique circumstances, some taxpayer groups will have their start date deferred or be permanently exempt from MTD:

One-year deferral (until April 2027): This applies to recipients of trust and estates income, individuals who use averaging adjustments, those eligible for qualifying care relief, and non-UK resident foreign entertainers or sportspeople. If you fall into one of these categories, and were theoretically required to use MTD as of April 2026, you should continue to meet your existing Self Assessment obligations as usual until April 2027.

Permanent exemptions: Businesses under a deputyship, as appointed by the Court of Protection, are now permanently exempt from MTD. This builds on the Spring Statement 2025 announcement that businesses who have a Power of Attorney are also exempt. If you fall under these criteria, you have clarity on your permanent exclusion from MTD requirements.

4. Policy and guidance updates

The journey to full MTD implementation is ongoing, so staying informed is key:

Legislation for the MTD for Income Tax updates was included in the Finance Bill 2025-26, which received Royal Assent as Finance Act 2026 on 18 March 2026.

Check HMRC’s guidance on GOV.UK for the latest position on the penalty easements and deferrals.

Check GOV.UK for HMRC’s latest update on the remaining restrictions that prevent certain taxpayers from signing up for mandatory MTD.

Why should you embrace MTD for Income Tax now?

Embracing MTD for Income Tax now gives you a real-time view of your income, expenses, and likely tax bill, which helps you manage cash flow and make better decisions.

Some may find the idea of quarterly updates onerous, but the core design of MTD is to provide you with a much clearer, more real-time understanding of your financial position.

Embracing MTD offers significant benefits that can genuinely transform your business’s financial health and decision-making.

Real-time visibility: By regularly updating your digital records and making quarterly updates, you gain a live snapshot of your income, expenses, and, crucially, your approximate tax liability. This eliminates the end-of-year scramble and the dreaded surprise tax bill.

Improved cash flow management: When you know roughly how much tax you’ll owe, you can put money aside consistently. This allows for far better financial planning, so you aren’t guesstimating your tax bill and risking a shortfall when it comes to buying a new van, investing in equipment, or simply covering personal expenses.

Smarter decisions: Accurate, up-to-date financial data also empowers you to make smarter business decisions. You can identify trends, understand your profitability throughout the year, and react promptly, rather than waiting for your accountant to crunch numbers months later.

Can you ignore quarterly updates during the soft landing period?

No. The soft landing only removes penalty points for late quarterly updates. Digital record-keeping, quarterly updates, and the tax return are all still required.

It’s not unnatural to think that, because there’s no penalties for late submission, you can simply ignore the first four quarterly updates, and simply file a digital tax return on 31 January 2028. 

While the penalty relief offers you flexibility, Chris Downing—Director of Accountants and Bookkeeping at Sage and a former accountant—offers a warning against postponing your MTD preparations:

“Firms shouldn’t mistake the soft landing for a free pass. The compliance obligations are still in force—digital recordkeeping, timely quarterly updates, and the full MTD Tax Return by January 2028. All the soft landing does is give you space to make mistakes safely. Ignoring that opportunity simply concentrates the risk later.”

If you use the penalty easement to deliberately skip updates or do a superficial job of record-keeping, you will also cheat yourself out of vital benefits:

You lose real-time visibility of your business, undermining the core advantage MTD offers for your cash flow and business planning.

Delaying the inevitable learning and compliance merely pushes the problem down the road. You’ll still have to switch to digital records and make sense of the system eventually, likely under more pressure. By then, the penalty-free soft landing period will have ended.

Grappling with a new system at the last minute significantly increases your risk of making errors or missing deadlines. Once the soft landing period concludes, the standard penalty regime takes full effect. Why not use this current grace period to master the system and build confidence, rather than deferring the pain and inviting potential penalties?

How does the MTD for Income Tax penalty points system work?

You get a penalty point for each late submission, and a £200 penalty once you reach your points threshold, which depends on how often you file.

It’s important to have a clear grasp of the penalty points system, which will be rolled out not only for MTD users but also for all Self Assessment taxpayers from April 2027.

Under the new system, simply filing a return late no longer triggers an automatic fine.

Instead, you’ll receive one penalty point every time you miss a submission deadline. This penalty applies only to the particular tax for which you’ve made the error. For example, if you miss an update for MTD for Income Tax, you might get penalty points. If you also miss a tax return date for VAT, you might also get points—but the two systems and points tallies are entirely separate.

Once you accumulate a certain number of these points—known as your personal points threshold—HMRC will then issue a £200 financial penalty. Every subsequent late submission will then incur an additional £200 charge.

Your points threshold depends on how often you’re required to submit returns.

Businesses that file more frequently have more opportunities to make mistakes, so their threshold is higher. For example, if you file annual tax returns, you’ll receive a penalty at two points. For quarterly filers, the penalty is issued at four points, and monthly filers have a threshold of five points.

These penalty points don’t stay on your record indefinitely. They expire after a period of good compliance, provided you’ve also submitted any outstanding returns. The length of this good compliance period also varies by your filing frequency. If you file annual tax returns, you’ll need to file on time for 24 months to clear your record. Quarterly filers must file on time for 12 months, and monthly filers need to file on time for six months.

Overall, this new system is designed to be more forgiving of genuine, one-off mistakes, giving you a chance to improve. However, it still takes persistent lateness seriously.

How should you prepare for MTD for Income Tax?

To prepare, check your start date, review your systems, choose MTD-compatible software, consider signing up voluntarily, and get professional advice.

Check your start date: Your first step is to determine your MTD start date. Confirm if your business was mandated for April 2026 or is mandated from April 2027 or April 2028 (based on the MTD thresholds), or if you qualify for a deferral or permanent exemption. This will set your personal timeline. If HMRC has already signed you up, read HMRC signed me up for MTD for Income Tax. What should I do now?

Evaluate your systems: Are you still using spreadsheets or a basic accounting system to manage your income and expenses? Assess how digital-ready your current methods are and identify what changes are needed.

Explore MTD-compatible software: Begin researching available software solutions that integrate with MTD for Income Tax. Many providers offer specific tools for sole traders. Consider trialling different options to find one that fits your workflow best.

Consider voluntary sign-up: You don’t have to wait, and can choose to voluntarily sign up for MTD now. This offers an excellent dry run opportunity. By starting early, you can become familiar with digital record-keeping and quarterly submissions, gaining valuable experience and confidence with the new system. If you’re due to start MTD for Income Tax in April 2027 or April 2028, signing up voluntarily now gives you a dry run. The government hasn’t yet confirmed whether the soft landing period will apply to those start dates. This early start is a fantastic way to refine your processes before mandatory adoption, ensuring you’re well-prepared from day one.

Get professional advice: Don’t hesitate to consult an accountant or tax adviser for professional advice. They can provide tailored guidance, help you choose and implement the right software, set up your new digital systems, and help you create a strategic plan for a smooth transition during the soft landing period.

Final thoughts on the MTD soft landing period

This MTD soft landing isn’t a delay. It’s a vital opportunity. With new flexibility around penalties and payment deadlines for your first year of MTD for Income Tax, sole traders and landlords now have a unique chance to prepare effectively.

By proactively preparing your digital systems, and potentially even opting for a voluntary “dry run” now, you can transform the challenge of MTD into an opportunity. Embrace this extra time to plan ahead, seek expert advice, and transition to digital record-keeping with confidence. Ultimately you will benefit from a clearer, more efficient view of your business’s finances.

MTD for Income Tax soft landing: FAQs

			

			

	

Is there a penalty for a late MTD quarterly update in the first year?

	

			

No penalty points apply to late quarterly updates in your first year if you were mandated from April 2026. Late submission of your first four quarterly updates (due between 7 August 2026 and 7 May 2027) doesn’t attract penalty points, provided other conditions are met.

	

	

Does the soft landing period cover the MTD tax return?

	

			

No. The soft landing period doesn’t cover the tax return, so penalties apply if your 2026/27 tax return isn’t submitted by 31 January 2028.

	

	

Does the soft landing period apply if I start MTD for Income Tax in April 2027?

	

			

The government hasn’t confirmed whether the soft landing period will apply to those starting in April 2027 or April 2028.

	

	

How many penalty points before I get an MTD penalty?

	

			

Quarterly filers, including those submitting MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates, get a £200 penalty at four points. Every later late submission adds another £200. Points expire after 12 months of on-time filing, provided any outstanding returns are submitted.

	

	

Do I still need to submit quarterly updates during the soft landing period?

	

			

Yes. HMRC still expects you to keep digital records from your MTD start date and to submit quarterly updates. The soft landing only removes penalty points for late submission. For more, read MTD quarterly updates: Everything you need to know.
